[{:db/id 17592186338791 :question/worked-solution "This time, we'll use $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ notation. First, we compute the derivative, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-3x+6\sqrt{x}) \\  & =2\cdot x-3+\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6{x}^{-1/2} \\  & =2x-3+3{x}^{-1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=4$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=4} & =2(4)-3+3(4)^{-1/2} \\  & =8-3+\frac{3}{2} \\  & =\frac{13}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve is $\frac{13}{2}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064259 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0be8176c-dc51-5ee3-ab7e-f7738c95222f" "question-2d253a70-5faa-50fb-9a2a-215f206560d5"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-0be8176c-dc51-5ee3-ab7e-f7738c95222f" :question/id #uuid "0be8176c-dc51-5ee3-ab7e-f7738c95222f" :question/math-academy-id "q-102233" :question/problem "Find the $x$-coordinate of the point on the curve $y=2{x}^{2}-2$ whose tangent has a slope of $2.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $f(x)=2{x}^{2}-2.$ The slope of the tangent at the point $x$ is equal to ${f}^{′}(x).$ Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}-2) \\  & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})-2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\  & =2\cdot 2x-0 \\  & =4x.\end{aligned}
$$

We now set ${f}^{′}(x)=2$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & =2 \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent is equal to $2$ at the point where $x=\frac{1}{2}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields #uuid "2d253a70-5faa-50fb-9a2a-215f206560d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-102235" :question/problem "Find the $x$-coordinate of the point on the curve $y={x}^{2}+2x+1$ whose tangent has a slope of $-2.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $f(x)={x}^{2}+2x+1.$ The slope of the tangent at the point $x$ is equal to ${f}^{′}(x).$ Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+2x+1) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\  & =2x+2\cdot 1+0 \\  & =2x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

We now set ${f}^{′}(x)=-2$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+2 & =-2 \\ 2x & =-2-2 \\ 2x & =-4 \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent is equal to $-2$ at the point where $x=-2.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ![](images/bc/bc5f763522aec68e97bef90126866fe6b2fe7246560d4dc9ddd2c71a5a524d88.png)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105758 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-aac4981c-3e93-5227-8d9f-16b46e3776f7" "question-f8583d4e-1a83-5981-bb25-84847566b1c0" "question-9d973ab4-2c91-51a2-bf21-8cc67388babd" "question-e0c88cba-2b84-5672-a20e-1cf48e9f5298" "question-daaf9013-5976-5a1b-a75f-74d8d2c1a5cd"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105610 :question/worked-solution "The polar equation $r=2a\sin\theta$ defines a circle of radius $|a|$ centered at the point $(0,a).$

In our case, we have $r=4\sin\theta,$ and therefore

$$
a = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2.
$$

Therefore, the equation $r=4\sin\theta$ gives a circle of radius $\left|2\right| = 2$ centered at the point $(0,2),$ as shown below.

![](images/a6/a6a1f74e065f3508c92f8a438eb1830aeb4f877c355cd7779e86183a0da92183.png)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105759 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-eb541cd2-06d9-513e-814b-43ef4f1b8af7" "question-06dd95dd-7aca-5dd6-bbfa-f6a3626f7868" "question-d345ebc0-fb4a-55bd-95ea-a1eddcced6e5" "question-7fdddd6d-d41d-5369-b195-6ee0cc2418de" "question-e14b9dd2-f663-55f7-a3e0-3b4821a83167"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105611 :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a circle of radius $|a| = |-4.5|=4.5$ centered at the point $(0,-4.5).$ 

In polar coordinates, the equation of such a circle is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =2a\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\cdot (-4.5)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =-9\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105761 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b69fb899-dda9-520e-9df1-5f655ac32f35" "question-2e8e220e-5d02-535f-8203-20819203c421" "question-5fff1012-20ae-54c4-8327-06d77bbed9eb" "question-0054ec1e-580f-564e-8493-248291e1368b"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105613 :question/problem "The polar curve $r=k\cos\theta,$ where $k$ is a constant, passes through the point $A$ with Cartesian coordinates $\left(-\dfrac72,\dfrac72\right).$ What is the value of $k?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the polar coordinates of the point $A.$ The distance from $A$ to the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{7}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{7\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $A$ lies in the second quadrant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|-\frac{(\frac{7}{2})}{(\frac{7}{2})}| \\  & =\pi -\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the polar coordinates of $A$ are $\left(r, \theta\right)=\left(\dfrac{7\sqrt{2}}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right).$ 

To find the value of $k$, we substitute the polar coordinates of the point $A$ into the polar equation of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =k\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{7\sqrt{2}}{2} & =k\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}) \\ \frac{7\sqrt{2}}{2} & =k(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\ k & =-7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the curve is $r=-7\cos\theta,$ as shown below.

![](images/8a/8aec18033a85129c44765d2670ebe9c931b0c0186c46b74f9b0ea0ae14028b76.png)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-9d2a01e3-0185-5503-82e9-9d6a8de6c36a" :question/id #uuid "9d2a01e3-0185-5503-82e9-9d6a8de6c36a" :question/math-academy-id "q-86983" :question/problem "Which of the following is the graph of the polar curve $r=2.5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ?$" :question/worked-solution "The polar equation $r=2a\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ defines a circle of radius $|a|$ centered at the point $(a,0).$

In our case, we have $r=2.5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ and therefore

$$
a=\frac{2.5}{2}=1.25.
$$

Therefore, the equation $r=2.5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ gives a circle of radius $|1.25|=1.25$ centered at the point $(1.25,0),$ as shown below.

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $A$ lies in the second quadrant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|-\frac{1}{1}| \\  & =\pi -\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the polar coordinates of $A$ are $(r,\theta )=(\sqrt{2},\frac{3\pi }{4}).$ 

To find the value of $k$, we substitute the polar coordinates of the point $A$ into the polar equation of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =k\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \sqrt{2} & =k\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}) \\ \sqrt{2} & =k(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}) \\ k & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the curve is $r=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ as shown below.

Therefore, the equation of the curve is $r=-6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ as shown below.

with Cartesian coordinates $(-3,\sqrt{3}),$  then $k=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "First, we find the polar coordinates of the point $A.$ The distance from $A$ to the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(-3)}^{2}+{(\sqrt{3})}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $A$ lies in the second quadrant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{\sqrt{3}}{-3}| \\  & =\pi -\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the polar coordinates of $A$ are $(r,\theta )=(2\sqrt{3},\frac{5\pi }{6}).$ 

To find the value of $k$, we substitute the polar coordinates of the point $A$ into the polar equation of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3} & =k\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 2\sqrt{3} & =k\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6}) \\ 2\sqrt{3} & =k(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\ k & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the curve is $r=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ as shown below.

![](images/de/def95f29f6397b0f6eab20afb6327d8f3f99fdc52fbeac0b0c2af8b228d060a9.png)" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6bbb16c8-6341-55ff-b300-2282e814f399"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-6bbb16c8-6341-55ff-b300-2282e814f399" :answer-field/id #uuid "6bbb16c8-6341-55ff-b300-2282e814f399" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-5351d84c-4882-5054-a0c1-cbc0e962e2cb" :answer-field/choices ["answer-5351d84c-4882-5054-a0c1-cbc0e962e2cb"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5351d84c-4882-5054-a0c1-cbc0e962e2cb" :answer/id #uuid "5351d84c-4882-5054-a0c1-cbc0e962e2cb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186107086 :tutorial/content "When a circle is not centered at the origin, we can still write its equation in polar form. In fact, the polar equation of a circle is particularly straightforward when it passes through the origin and its center lies on the $x$-axis.

For example, let $a$ be some nonzero real number, and consider a circle of radius $|a|$ with center at the point $(a,0)$. 

![](images/46/4632ae0baaced6ba3699fddf859b71226b5fcebe4700bbbdf4774d1d701e53ad.png)

With a little bit of geometry and trigonometry, it turns out that the equation of this circle in polar form is given by

$$
r=2a\cos\theta.
$$

We'll derive this result at the end of the lesson.

So, for instance, if $a=2$, then we have a circle of radius $2$ centered at $(2,0),$ and its polar equation is

$$
r= 4 \cos\theta.
$$

Similarly, if $a=-2,$ then we have a circle of radius $|{-2}| = 2$ centered at $(-2,0),$ and its polar equation is

$$
r= -4 \cos\theta.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186107087 :tutorial/content "Now, let $a$ be some nonzero real number, and let's consider a circle of radius $|a|$ whose center is at the point $(0,a).$

![](images/40/40477171cd880e675656ed0093c26a85ebe02b7939ec9421a1bcc52c763a68fe.png)

Notice that this circle passes through the origin, and its center lies on the $y$-axis.

Again, using some geometry and trigonometry, it's possible to show that the polar equation of the circle is

$$
r=2a \sin \theta.
$$

We'll derive this result at the end of the lesson.

So, for instance, if $a=2,$ then we have a circle of radius $2$ centered at $(0,2),$ and its polar equation is

$$
r=4 \sin \theta.
$$

Similarly, if $a=-3$, then we have a circle of radius $|{-3}| = 3$ centered at $(0,-3),$ and its polar equation is

$$
r=-6 \sin \theta.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186107028 :tutorial/content "![](images/46/4632ae0baaced6ba3699fddf859b71226b5fcebe4700bbbdf4774d1d701e53ad.png)

Suppose we want to derive the polar equation of a circle with

- center at $(a, 0)$, where $a \ne 0$, and

- radius $|a|$, so that it passes through the origin.

Let a point $P$ on the circle have polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$. Then, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are

$$
(x, y) = (r\cos\theta, \, r\sin\theta).
$$

The distance from $P$ to the center $(a, 0)$ is equal to the radius $|a|.$ We can describe this using the distance formula:

$$
\sqrt{(r\cos\theta - a)^2 + (r\sin\theta)^2} = |a|
$$

Squaring both sides, we get

$$
(r\cos\theta - a)^2 + (r\sin\theta)^2 = a^2.
$$

Expanding both terms yields

$$
r^2\cos^2\theta - 2ar\cos\theta + a^2 + r^2\sin^2\theta = a^2.
$$

Then, we combine like terms:

$$
r^2(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta) - 2ar\cos\theta + a^2 = a^2
$$

Since $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$, we can simplify the above as follows:

$$
r^2 - 2ar\cos\theta + a^2 = a^2
$$

Subtracting $a^2$ from both sides gives

$$
r^2 - 2ar\cos\theta = 0.
$$

Then, we factor our equation:

$$
r(r - 2a\cos\theta) = 0
$$

So, either $r = 0$ (which corresponds to the origin, already on the circle), or

$$
r = 2a\cos\theta,
$$

which is the desired polar equation of the circle." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186107029 :tutorial/content "![](images/a2/a2662be5d74155ca29b600cf48982a1ee2b0db62459334af7784394cabea8687.png)

Suppose we want to derive the polar equation of a circle with

- center at $(0, a)$, where $a \ne 0$, and

- radius $|a|$, so that it passes through the origin.

Let a point $P$ on the circle have polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$. Then, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are

$$
(x, y) = (r\cos\theta, \, r\sin\theta).
$$

The distance from $P$ to the center $(0, a)$ is equal to the radius $|a|.$ We can describe this using the distance formula:

$$
\sqrt{(r\cos\theta - 0)^2 + (r\sin\theta - a)^2} = |a|
$$

Squaring both sides, we get

$$
(r\cos\theta)^2 + (r\sin\theta - a)^2 = a^2.
$$

Expanding both terms yields

$$
r^2\cos^2\theta + r^2\sin^2\theta - 2ar\sin\theta + a^2 = a^2.
$$

Then, we combine like terms:

$$
r^2(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta) - 2ar\sin\theta + a^2 = a^2
$$

Since $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$, we simplify:

$$
r^2 - 2ar\sin\theta + a^2 = a^2
$$

Subtracting $a^2$ from both sides gives

$$
r^2 - 2ar\sin\theta = 0.
$$

Then, we factor our equation:

$$
r(r - 2a\sin\theta) = 0
$$

So, either $r = 0$ (which corresponds to the origin, already on the circle), or

$$
r = 2a\sin\theta,
$$

which is the desired polar equation of the circle." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105952 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068732 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-eeaf419f-60bd-5e26-a56f-c339e863386b" "question-a79b6cc2-bbc0-53f7-9fa7-3b0e82f61fd9"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-eeaf419f-60bd-5e26-a56f-c339e863386b" :question/id #uuid "eeaf419f-60bd-5e26-a56f-c339e863386b" :question/math-academy-id "q-80" :question/problem "Solve the equation ${3}^{y}=81.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we rewrite $81$ as ${3}^{4}$ to get:

"First, we isolate the term with the variable exponent by dividing both sides by $2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot {8}^{y} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{2\cdot {8}^{y}}{2} & =\frac{(\frac{1}{4})}{2} \\ {8}^{y} & =\frac{1}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rewrite $\frac{1}{8}$ as ${8}^{-1}$ to get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{8}^{y} & =\frac{1}{8} \\ {8}^{y} & ={8}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since both sides of the equation share the same base $(8)$, we equate the exponents:

$$
\begin{aligned}{8}^{y} & ={8}^{-1} \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $y=-1.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cd01a93c-d6e2-540b-8c0d-44c14937bd8f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} "ea6c80e5-0a00-5798-9872-7c227f663338" :question/math-academy-id "q-5158" :question/problem "Factor $162{x}^{4}-2.$" :question/worked-solution "The difference of squares formula is given by

$$
{a}^{2}-{b}^{2}=(a+b)(a-b)
$$

Notice that all of the terms have a common factor of $2.$ To simplify the computation, we can factor out the $2,$ as follows:

$$
162{x}^{4}-2=2\cdot 81{x}^{4}-2\cdot 1=2(81{x}^{4}-1)
$$

The expression in parentheses can be written as a difference of squares:

$$
2(81{x}^{4}-1)=2({(9{x}^{2})}^{2}-{1}^{2})
$$

Now, we factor our expression using the difference of squares formula:

$$
2({(9{x}^{2})}^{2}-{1}^{2})=2(9{x}^{2}+1)(9{x}^{2}-1)
$$

:question/id #uuid "66207faf-3d6b-5406-8c58-c05d9d84a48f" :question/math-academy-id "q-95283" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

I. The matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-10 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ has one negative singular value.

II. Any $2\times 4$ matrix $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

III. Any $6\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $6$ distinct singular values." :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false.  All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, 
$A$  can't have any negative singular value.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,  since $A$ is a $2\times 4$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $4\times 2$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $4\times 4$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{4\times 2}\times {A}_{2\times 4}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{4\times 4}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is false. Since $A$ is a $6\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a29f2b28-9204-5899-8070-b3f5ffe02498"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a29f2b28-9204-5899-8070-b3f5ffe02498" :answer-field/id #uuid "a29f2b28-9204-5899-8070-b3f5ffe02498" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-aa4333dc-3ea2-5e37-ab50-ec3e34c12a9e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-db2d98c7-af14-5f48-be6c-f11b82999c7b" "answer-1d848745-0d69-5731-947e-0a9ae11809b4" "answer-09638aaf-77e9-5651-870e-522b6cc8115f" "answer-aa4333dc-3ea2-5e37-ab50-ec3e34c12a9e" "answer-c588edce-5cf5-501a-93b4-d2734b483461"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-db2d98c7-af14-5f48-be6c-f11b82999c7b" :answer/id #uuid "db2d98c7-af14-5f48-be6c-f11b82999c7b" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1d848745-0d69-5731-947e-0a9ae11809b4" :answer/id #uuid "1d848745-0d69-5731-947e-0a9ae11809b4" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-09638aaf-77e9-5651-870e-522b6cc8115f" :answer/id #uuid "09638aaf-77e9-5651-870e-522b6cc8115f" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-aa4333dc-3ea2-5e37-ab50-ec3e34c12a9e" :answer/id #uuid "aa4333dc-3ea2-5e37-ab50-ec3e34c12a9e" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c588edce-5cf5-501a-93b4-d2734b483461" :answer/id #uuid "c588edce-5cf5-501a-93b4-d2734b483461" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-1e0723ce-a987-5c3e-a185-24b9f3aa7c5c" :question/id #uuid "1e0723ce-a987-5c3e-a185-24b9f3aa7c5c" :question/math-academy-id "q-95270" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

I. Any $3\times 4$ matrix $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

II. Any $8\times 6$ matrix $A$ has at most $8$ distinct singular values.

III. The matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]$ has one negative singular value." :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Since $A$ is a $3\times 4$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $4\times 3$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $4\times 4$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{4\times 3}\times {A}_{3\times 4}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{4\times 4}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. Since $A$ is a $8\times 6$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $6\times 8$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $6\times 6$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{6\times 8}\times {A}_{8\times 6}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{6\times 6}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $6$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is false.  All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, 
$A$  can't have a negative singular value.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0c3c93af-58f9-530c-baad-0a629ae81ede"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-0c3c93af-58f9-530c-baad-0a629ae81ede" :answer-field/id #uuid "0c3c93af-58f9-530c-baad-0a629ae81ede" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-79ac5216-69de-5dc4-a92b-b636df49e5d3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-026e9975-ba0c-5eae-815a-fcd1e665b3d2" "answer-79ac5216-69de-5dc4-a92b-b636df49e5d3" "answer-7f21a217-b4f0-55ce-b377-f084a5b14d24" "answer-e014b07e-27e4-516d-adc5-1ef689408d39" "answer-c2c913d4-93f7-5765-8bb6-090f7d52622b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-026e9975-ba0c-5eae-815a-fcd1e665b3d2" :answer/id #uuid "026e9975-ba0c-5eae-815a-fcd1e665b3d2" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-79ac5216-69de-5dc4-a92b-b636df49e5d3" :answer/id #uuid "79ac5216-69de-5dc4-a92b-b636df49e5d3" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7f21a217-b4f0-55ce-b377-f084a5b14d24" :answer/id #uuid "7f21a217-b4f0-55ce-b377-f084a5b14d24" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e014b07e-27e4-516d-adc5-1ef689408d39" :answer/id #uuid "e014b07e-27e4-516d-adc5-1ef689408d39" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c2c913d4-93f7-5765-8bb6-090f7d52622b" :answer/id #uuid "c2c913d4-93f7-5765-8bb6-090f7d52622b" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185322 :tutorial/content "Recall that the singular values of a real matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

Also, since $A^T \! A$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A$ must be always non-negative real numbers.

Let's compute the singular values of the matrix $A,$ given by 

![](images/a9/a9edbe1fee59758c9557d95ea8f62468f9f3cb98449c437a274bdbf5c30f7dc6.svg)

Now, since

- $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and

- $A^T$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix,

then $A^T \! A$  must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix:

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.

- If $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T A$ is a $n\times n$ positive semi-definite matrix. This means that $A$ has *at most* $n$ distinct singular values." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186365845 :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-20\lambda {y}^{′}+100{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,y(0)=0,\,y\,(\frac{1}{2})+{y}^{′}\,(\frac{1}{2})=0,\,0\le x\le \frac{1}{2},\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166940 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-648c7fb6-34ca-53e3-ba2b-a6cf79213062"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-648c7fb6-34ca-53e3-ba2b-a6cf79213062" :question/id #uuid "648c7fb6-34ca-53e3-ba2b-a6cf79213062" :question/math-academy-id "q-338913" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+49{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(2)=0,\,0\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$" :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields $A=0.$ Thus, we have a nontrivial solution, so $\lambda =0$ is a parameter corresponding to the eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+49{\lambda }^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 7\text{i}\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\lambda x),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\lambda x)
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\lambda x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\lambda x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}=-7A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(7\lambda x)+7B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(7\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
-7A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+7B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $B=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
-7A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(14\lambda )=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
14\lambda =n\pi 
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{14}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7{\lambda }_{n}x),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9c89b6fc-2543-5375-ab12-8c5c3b4ded4d" "answer-field-9f0c0ee2-17d3-59de-a732-734f1a510b76"] :db/ensure We can do this using the **quotient rule**. 

The quotient rule is very similar to the product rule, except that this time we're dealing with the difference of two logarithms rather than the sum. 

The quotient rule states that two logarithms which share a common base $\color{blue}n$ satisfy

$$
\log_{\color{blue}n} (a) - \log_{\color{blue}n} (b) = \log_{\color{blue}n}\left(\dfrac a b\right) .
$$

So, we can use this rule to rewrite $\log_{\color{blue}3}(4) - \log_{\color{blue}3}(6)$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡(4)-{log}_{3}⁡(6) & ={log}_{3}⁡(\frac{4}{6}) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(\frac{2}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

The quotient rule works exactly the same for the natural and common logarithms." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110843 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092172 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-597abfab-9fa0-5884-9650-9d3a1ca7b418" "question-7afac99d-b74c-555b-b269-d08cbbf29447" "question-c08c7d82-b9b5-59ff-a4f6-2f1eac5d7e57" "question-bf7fd672-fd24-5897-b0f7-1572fe68c96d" "question-44457776-708f-510a-afa3-90718ee8b770"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186091991 :question/problem "Consider the equation $\cos{2x} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ for $0\leq x < 2\pi.$ If the solutions $x_1, x_2, x_3$ and $x_4$ are written in ascending order,  what is the value of $x_2\cdot x_3?$" :question/worked-solution "We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =\frac{\pi }{4}+2n\pi , & \, & \, & 2x & =\frac{7\pi }{4}+2n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Solving our two equations for $x$ gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{\pi }{8}+n\pi  & \, & \, & x & =\frac{7\pi }{8}+n\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{8}+\frac{8n\pi }{8} & \, & \, & x & =\frac{7\pi }{8}+\frac{8n\pi }{8} \\ x & =\frac{(8n+1)\pi }{8} & \, & \, & x & =\frac{(8n+7)\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0, \pm 1, \pm 2,\ldots,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $0 \leq x \lt 2\pi.$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ and $x=\dfrac{7\pi}{8}.$

- Setting $n=1$ gives $x=\dfrac{9\pi}{8}$ and $x=\dfrac{15\pi}{8}.$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $0 \leq x \lt 2\pi.$ So, the solutions $x_1, x_2, x_3$ and $x_4$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x = \dfrac{\pi}{8}, \, \dfrac{7\pi}{8}, \, \dfrac{9\pi}{8}, \, \dfrac{15\pi}{8}.
$$

Finally, 

$$
x_2\cdot x_3 =  \dfrac{7\pi}{8} \cdot  \dfrac{9\pi}{8} = \dfrac{63\pi^2}{64}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092173 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0663d30d-9045-55b3-9c5e-7d0dcf4eda51" "question-689ab27d-73f0-5878-911e-f4bfe8b4c90e" "question-cd740014-1051-58c1-bf02-d54c44856f2e" "question-468c5cf8-2c4e-5dd6-96eb-d94e2d3f4648" "question-9acc1f61-f727-5595-afa3-5b687cb64df5"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186091993 :question/problem "Solve the equation $-2\sqrt{3}\cos\left(2x+60^\circ\right) - 3 = 0$ for $0^\circ\leq x <           360^\circ.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+{60}^{∘})-3 & =0 \\ -2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+{60}^{∘}) & =3 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+{60}^{∘}) & =-\frac{3}{2\sqrt{3}} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+{60}^{∘}) & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We will find the general solution to the equation and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+{60}^{∘} & ={150}^{∘}+n\cdot {360}^{∘}, & \, & \, & 2x+{60}^{∘} & ={210}^{∘}+n\cdot {360}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the two equations above for $x$ gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & ={150}^{∘}-{60}^{∘}+n\cdot {360}^{∘} & \, & \, & 2x & ={210}^{∘}-{60}^{∘}+n\cdot {360}^{∘} \\ 2x & ={90}^{∘}+n\cdot {360}^{∘} & \, & \, & 2x & ={150}^{∘}+n\cdot {360}^{∘} \\ x & ={45}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘} & \, & \, & x & ={75}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0, \pm 1, \pm 2,\ldots$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $0^\circ \leq x \lt 360^\circ.$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=45^\circ$ and $x=75^\circ.$

- Setting $n=1$ gives $x=225^\circ$  and $x=255^\circ.$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $0^\circ \leq x \lt 360^\circ.$ So, the solutions $x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x_1 = 45^\circ,\quad x_2 = 75^\circ,\quad x_3 =  225^\circ,\quad x_4= 255^\circ .

{x}_{3}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5x}{2})+3 & =0 \\ 2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5x}{2}) & =-3 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5x}{2}) & =-\frac{3}{2\sqrt{3}} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5x}{2}) & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5x}{2} & =\frac{5\pi }{6}+2n\pi , & \, & \, & \frac{5x}{2} & =\frac{7\pi }{6}+2n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the two equations above for $x$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x & =\frac{5\pi }{3}+4n\pi  & \, & \, & 5x & =\frac{7\pi }{3}+4n\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{4n\pi }{5} & \, & \, & x & =\frac{7\pi }{15}+\frac{4n\pi }{5} \\ x & =\frac{(12n+5)\pi }{15} & \, & \, & x & =\frac{(12n+7)\pi }{15}\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $0\le x<2\pi .$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=\frac{\pi }{3}$ and $x=\frac{7\pi }{15}$

- Setting $n=1$ gives $x=\frac{17\pi }{15}$  and $x=\frac{19\pi }{15}.$

- Setting $n=2$ gives $x=\frac{29\pi }{15}$  and $x=\frac{31\pi }{15}.$ We reject the solution $\frac{31\pi }{15}$ since it lies outside the domain of interest.

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $0\le x<2\pi .$ So, the solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4},{x}_{5}$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x=\frac{\pi }{3},\,\frac{7\pi }{15},\,\frac{17\pi }{15},\,\frac{19\pi }{15},\,\frac{29\pi }{15}.
$$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{3}=\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot \frac{17\pi }{15}=\frac{17{\pi }^{2}}{45}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-babdd4ab-5b3d-5b5f-8892-4e5632d1283f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c6635c31-8a89-581f-88ba-c9350baa70ca"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-c6635c31-8a89-581f-88ba-c9350baa70ca" :answer-field/id #uuid "c6635c31-8a89-581f-88ba-c9350baa70ca" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-edf9637c-aede-513e-8154-e840c0b4d689" :answer-field/choices ["answer-da5f6ffe-39d2-5021-9518-42610f548da9" "answer-33d9c60f-2f9d-53f4-980f-9aa97023962f" "answer-edf9637c-aede-513e-8154-e840c0b4d689" "answer-d7168513-56cb-58e5-b423-239ea3770fba" "answer-18eb997a-9844-5aac-b91f-00f5f300d39b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-da5f6ffe-39d2-5021-9518-42610f548da9" :answer/id #uuid "da5f6ffe-39d2-5021-9518-42610f548da9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7\pi }{12}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-33d9c60f-2f9d-53f4-980f-9aa97023962f" :answer/id #uuid "33d9c60f-2f9d-53f4-980f-9aa97023962f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7{\pi }^{2}}{24}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-edf9637c-aede-513e-8154-e840c0b4d689" :answer/id #uuid "edf9637c-aede-513e-8154-e840c0b4d689" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7{\pi }^{2}}{48}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d7168513-56cb-58e5-b423-239ea3770fba" :answer/id #uuid "d7168513-56cb-58e5-b423-239ea3770fba" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{48}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-18eb997a-9844-5aac-b91f-00f5f300d39b" :answer/id #uuid "18eb997a-9844-5aac-b91f-00f5f300d39b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{24}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186093391 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find all of the solutions to

$$
\cos\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}, 
	\qquad -\pi \leq x < \pi.
$$

Notice that the equation contains a transformed cosine function. 

We know that the general solution to the elementary equation $\cos{X} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =\frac{\pi }{3}+2n\pi , & \, & \, & X & =\frac{5\pi }{3}+2n\pi ,\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is assumed to be any integer.

To find the general solution of the transformed cosine equation, we replace $X$ with the input of the cosine function, which is $x + \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ in this case. This gives the general solution 

$$
x+\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{3} + 2n\pi, \qquad\qquad x+\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}+ 2n\pi.
$$

We now solve the above two equations for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2n\pi  & \, & \, & x & =\frac{4\pi }{3}+2n\pi  \\  &  & \, & \, & x & =\frac{4\pi }{3}+\frac{6n\pi }{3} \\  &  & \, & \, & x & =\frac{2\pi (2+3n)}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set $n = 0, \pm1, \pm2, \ldots$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $-\pi \leq x < \pi.$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}.$ We reject the solution $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ since it lies outside the domain of interest.

- Setting $n=-1$ gives $x=-2\pi$ and $x=-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}.$ We reject the solution $-2\pi$ since it lies outside the domain of interest.

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $-\pi \leq x < \pi.$ So, the solutions $x_1$ and $x_2$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x_1 = -\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\qquad x_2 = 0.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092424 :activity/expected-seconds 1320.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176033 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d6509173-6968-54cb-999d-d5fe096ebbff" "question-f1b17b2b-5f71-5d88-80f9-025ec7f6d205" "question-b2848e9c-e485-5752-8daf-a5d57b496ccb"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-d6509173-6968-54cb-999d-d5fe096ebbff" :question/id #uuid "d6509173-6968-54cb-999d-d5fe096ebbff" :question/math-academy-id "q-134798" :question/problem "![](images/b3/b375c1e162a9f1c2892903c20606921673498579f9b41f633447832fd3ea2192.png)

The scatter plot for the data sets $x$ and $y$ of paired observations and the corresponding linear regression line are shown above.

According to the regression model, what is the residual for the highlighted datapoint?" :question/worked-solution "The residual equals the difference between the actual value of the dependent variable and the value estimated using the linear regression model:

$$
\text{Residual}=\text{Actual}-\text{Estimated}
$$

 

The highlighted datapoint has coordinates $(4,70).$ So, our actual value is $y=70.$

On the other hand, the point on the regression line that corresponds to $x=4$ has the $y$-coordinate $50.$ So, our estimated value of is $\overset{^}{y}=50.$

Therefore, the residual is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Residual} & =\text{Actual}-\text{Estimated} \\  & =y-\overset{^}{y} \\  & =70-50 \\  & =20.\end{aligned}

"question-b2848e9c-e485-5752-8daf-a5d57b496ccb" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281623 :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M$ occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2\}.$
The mass density at each point is proportional to its distance from the $y$-axis.
Find the moment of inertia of the lamina about the origin." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281670 :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that the region $D,$ in polar coordinates, can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

From the description, the mass density function can be written as $\lambda (r,\theta )=kr,$ where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find an expression for $k$ in terms of $M$ by integrating the density function over the plate:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}kr\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}k{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =k({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =k\cdot \frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}\,{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =k\cdot \frac{7}{3}\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =\frac{14\pi k}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=kr=\frac{3M}{14\pi }r.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{3M}{14\pi }r\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2}\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}\,{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\theta +\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }\cdot \frac{31}{5}\cdot \pi  \\  & =\frac{93M}{70}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "activity-fbfee663-8b23-548a-9017-c32bfd0341c2" :activity/id #uuid "fbfee663-8b23-548a-9017-c32bfd0341c2" :activity/title "Moments of Inertia of Laminas $$

- reducing the dataset to $1$ dimension would preserve $65.8%$ of the variance, while

$$

{{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "In reducing the dimensionality of the dataset, we aim to preserve as much of the original variance as possible. 

We should pick components based on $\text{the amount of cumulative variance preserved}.$

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

In our example, the singular values are

$$
{\sigma }_{1}=3.067,\,{\sigma }_{2}=1.933,\,{\sigma }_{3}=1.517,\,{\sigma }_{4}=0.763.
$$

Let us now compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 

$$
\frac{{\sigma }_{1}^{2}}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}=\frac{{3.067}^{2}}{{3.067}^{2}+{1.933}^{2}+{1.517}^{2}+{0.763}^{2}}≈58.7%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 

$$
\frac{{\sum }_{i=1}^{2}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}=\frac{{3.067}^{2}+{1.933}^{2}}{{3.067}^{2}+{1.933}^{2}+{1.517}^{2}+{0.763}^{2}}≈82.0%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first three principal components is 

$$
\frac{{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}=\frac{{3.067}^{2}+{1.933}^{2}+{1.517}^{2}}{{3.067}^{2}+{1.933}^{2}+{1.517}^{2}+{0.763}^{2}}≈96.4%.
$$

Thus, we obtain that

- reducing the dataset to $1$ dimension would preserve $58.7%$ of the variance,

- reducing the dataset to $2$ dimensions would preserve $82.0%$ of the variance, while

- reducing the dataset to $3$ dimensions would preserve $96.4%$ of the variance.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}}{8}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{8}-\frac{(-4)^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{8}-1 & =1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{8} & =1+1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{8} & =2 \\ {y}^{2} & =16 \\ y & =\pm 4\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem "By expressing $\ln\left(x^2\right)$ in the form $k\ln x,$ determine the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the power rule for logarithms:

$$
\log_n(c^m)= m\log_n\left( c \right)
$$

Using the power rule for logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k =2.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110597 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-9f684a9a-73a2-5a55-8105-9ed436326180" "question-b071d322-d430-5f91-b157-0d44ee6fac29"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110498 :question/problem "By expressing $\dfrac{1}{2}\log_3{x}$ in the form $\log_3 \left(x^k\right),$ determine the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the power rule for logarithms:

$$
\log_n(c^m)= m\log_n\left( c \right)
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{log}_{3}⁡x & ={log}_{3}⁡({x}^{1/2}).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\operatorname{log}⁡({c}^{m})=m\operatorname{log}⁡(c)
$$

Using the power rule for logarithms, the given expression can be rewritten as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}⁡\sqrt{6x} & =\operatorname{log}⁡((6x)^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{log}⁡(6x)\end{aligned}

It states that

$$
\log_{n}\left( c^{\color{blue}m} \right) = {\color{blue}m}\log_{n}{c}.
$$

In other words, the logarithm has the effect of "bringing down the power."

For example, let's use the rule to simplify $\log\left(125\right)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}⁡(125) & =\operatorname{log}⁡({5}^{3}) \\  & =3\operatorname{log}⁡(5)\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** To understand why the power rule works, notice that we can reach the same result using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}⁡(125) & =\operatorname{log}⁡({5}^{3}) \\  & =\operatorname{log}⁡(5\cdot 5\cdot 5) \\  & =\operatorname{log}⁡(5)+\operatorname{log}⁡(5)+\operatorname{log}⁡(5) \\  & =3\operatorname{log}⁡(5)\end{aligned}
$$

The power rule is just a shortcut for the above procedure." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110844 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186107763 :answer-field/choices 17592186107764] [:db/retract 17592186107763 :answer-field/choices 17592186107765] [:db/retract 17592186107763 :answer-field/choices 17592186107766] [:db/retract 17592186107763 :answer-field/choices 17592186107767] [:db/retract 17592186108617 :answer-field/choices 17592186108618] [:db/retract 17592186108617 :answer-field/choices 17592186108619] [:db/retract 17592186108617 :answer-field/choices 17592186108620] [:db/retract 17592186108617 :answer-field/choices 17592186108621] [:db/retract 17592186108617 :answer-field/choices 17592186108622] {:db/id 17592186110682 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-f95ce679-5df8-536b-9a6e-bc83e05e288c" "question-81da0bad-95e8-53a0-9f19-ddc55b628c5f" "question-5c63aa2a-bac5-5697-a40d-14aec41163e5" "question-eb877a39-4dd4-5455-8e16-f850f269ea03" "question-4a638344-d920-5adc-900d-8c273723b689"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110462 :question/problem "Consider the equation $\sqrt{3}\sin{\theta }\tan{\theta }-\sin{\theta } = 0$ for $0^\circ \leq \theta <  360^\circ.$ If the solutions $\theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3, \theta_4$ are written in ascending order, then what is the numerical value of $\theta_2\cdot \theta_3?$" :question/worked-solution "Note that the function $\tan{\theta}$ is not defined at $\theta = 90^\circ , 270^\circ,$ so these values cannot be solutions to the equation. 

First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (\sqrt{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

By the zero-product property, we have to solve two equations: 

$$
\sin{\theta } = 0, \qquad \sqrt{3}\tan{\theta } - 1 =0.
$$

Let's solve each equation separately.

- First, we solve $\sin{\theta} = 0.$ The solutions to this equation for $0^\circ \leq \theta <  360^\circ$  are $\theta = 0^\circ, \, 180^\circ.$

- Then, we solve $\sqrt{3}\tan{\theta } - 1 =0,$ or equivalently $\tan{\theta} =  \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.$ The solutions to this equation for $0^\circ \leq \theta <  360^\circ$ are $\theta=30^\circ, \, 210^\circ.$

Combining all solutions from both equations, we get

$$
\theta_1 = 0^\circ, \quad \theta_2= 30^\circ, \quad \theta_3=180^\circ, \quad \theta_4= 210^\circ.
$$

Finally, 

$$
\theta_2\cdot \theta_3 =30 \cdot  180 = 5\,400.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110683 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-df0bb882-2469-5cab-82f5-df4eee26a54c" "question-49fd94b7-d87e-5482-b74a-14a44acf4a47" "question-df31d07c-21a6-58c5-a19d-926033829f92" "question-0135fc07-6118-52f5-9b57-2dcf9eca07ac"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110461 :question/problem "Consider the equation $\sqrt{2} \sin{x} \cos{x} = -\sin{x}$ for $0 \leq x \leq \pi.$ If the solutions $x_1, x_2, x_3$ are written in ascending order, then what is $x_2\cdot x_3?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

By the zero-product property, we have to solve two equations: 

$$
\sin{x} = 0, \qquad \sqrt{2} \cos{x} + 1 =0.
$$

Let's solve each equation separately.

- First, we solve $\sin{x} = 0.$ The solutions to this equation for $0\leq x \leq \pi$  are $x = 0,\, \pi.$

- Then, we solve $\sqrt{2} \cos{x} + 1= 0,$ or equivalently $\cos{x} =-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.$ The solution to this equation for $0\leq x \leq \pi$  is $x =\dfrac{3\pi}{4}.$

Combining all solutions from both equations, we get

$$
x_1 = 0,\quad x_2=\dfrac{3\pi}{4},\quad x_3= \pi.
$$

Finally, 

$$
x_2\cdot x_3 = \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \cdot  \pi=\dfrac{3\pi^2}{4}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110684 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a135a2c5-e84d-52d5-89de-19fd76614f68" "question-68f4987d-ed26-5738-89d9-828f518f37d4" "question-fc1ed235-5329-5107-b309-feec267a8cde" "question-cf8eafa9-ba3d-54d7-ae84-18acaa32c81c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110463 :question/problem "Solve the equation $\csc{x} \tan{x} = \tan{x}$ for $0^\circ \leq x <  360^\circ.$" :question/worked-solution "Note that the function $\csc{x}$ is not defined at the points where $\sin{x} = 0.$ On the interval $0^\circ \leq x <  360^\circ,$ the excluded values are $x = 0^\circ , 180^\circ.$

On the other hand, the function $\tan{x}$ is not defined at the points where $\cos{x} = 0.$ In the given interval, the excluded values are $x = 90^\circ , 270^\circ.$

First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ \operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =0 \\ (\operatorname{csc}⁡x-1)\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the zero-product property, we have to solve two equations: 

$$
\csc{x} - 1 = 0, \qquad \tan{x} = 0
$$

Let's solve each equation separately.

- First, we solve $\csc{x} -1= 0,$ or equivalently, $\csc x=1.$ The solution to this equation for $0 ^\circ \leq x \lt 360^\circ$ is $x = 90^\circ.$

- Then, we solve $\tan{x} = 0.$ The solutions to this equation for $0^\circ\leq x \lt 360^\circ$  are $x = 0^\circ,\, 180^\circ.$

Finally, taking into account the values excluded from the interval, we conclude that the given equation has no solution." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110685 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-22a4714b-c9b9-595d-bd56-cdf122336677" "question-aa82973f-2912-57c5-acdd-b4b8b9abbe44"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110464 :question/problem "The graph shows the curve $y = 2\sin{x}\cos{x}$ and the curve $y = \cos{x}$ on the interval $0^\circ \leq x < 360^\circ.$ The curves intersect at the points $A,$ $B,$ $C,$ and $D,$ as shown. Find $x$-coordinates of these points.

![](images/d3/d3462ebb123dcaf59391787ffae5b39dea5809eefe656cfda2f17498259dc1b6.png)" :question/worked-solution "At the intersection points, the $y$ values of both graphs are the same. This gives 
the equation

$$
2\sin{x}\cos{x} = \cos{x}.
$$

First, we factor the equation:

{{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x(2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\sqrt{3}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the zero-product property, we have to solve two equations:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡x=0,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\sqrt{3}=0
$$

Let's solve each equation separately.

- First, we solve $\operatorname{sin}⁡x=0.$ The solutions to this equation for $-\pi \le x<\pi $ are $x=-\pi ,\,0.$

- Then, we solve $2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\sqrt{3}=0,$ or equivalently $\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$ The solutions to this equation for $-\pi \le x<\pi $ are $x=-\frac{\pi }{6},\,\frac{\pi }{6}.$

Arranging all solutions from both equations in ascending order, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\pi ,\,{x}_{2}=-\frac{\pi }{6},\,{x}_{3}=0,\,{x}_{4}=\frac{\pi }{6}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-be519b0a-648a-5300-b22a-fd5381ebda77" "answer-field-76c89bcd-2113-5515-8496-363099c12112" ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4}$ are written in ascending order, then what is the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x(2\operatorname{cos}⁡x+1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡x=0,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡x+1=0
$$

$$

$$

$$
{x}_{1}=0,\,{x}_{2}=\pi .

On the other hand, the function $\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ is not defined at the points where $\operatorname{cos}⁡x=0.$ On the interval $-\pi \le x<\pi ,$ the excluded values are $x=-\frac{\pi }{2},\,\frac{\pi }{2}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{csc}⁡x+\operatorname{tan}⁡x-2\operatorname{csc}⁡x-1 & =0 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x(2\operatorname{csc}⁡x+1)-(2\operatorname{csc}⁡x+1) & =0 \\ (2\operatorname{csc}⁡x+1)(\operatorname{tan}⁡x-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the zero-product property, we have to solve two equations: 

$$
2\operatorname{csc}⁡x+1=0,\,\operatorname{tan}⁡x-1=0
$$

Let's solve each equation separately.

- First, we solve $2\operatorname{csc}⁡x+1=0,$ or equivalently $\operatorname{sin}⁡x=-2.$ But since $|\operatorname{sin}⁡x|\le 1,$ then $\operatorname{sin}⁡x=2$ has no solution.

- Then, we solve $\operatorname{tan}⁡x-1=0,$ or equivalently $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=1.$ The solutions to this equation for $-\pi \le x<\pi $ are $x=-\frac{3\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4}.$

Combining all solutions from both equations, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{3\pi }{4},\,{x}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$

Finally, 

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=-\frac{3\pi }{4}\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}=-\frac{3{\pi }^{2}}{16}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-391ba5d5-1569-5749-804d-be4aff1f7cf2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
\sin{x}\cos{x}-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin{x} = 0,  \qquad 0^\circ \leq x \leq 180^\circ.
$$

First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\frac{1}{2}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can now apply the zero product rule, which states that $ab=0$ if and only if $a=0$ or $b=0.$ This gives us two equations,

$$
\sin{x} = 0 \quad \textrm{and} \quad \cos{x}-\dfrac12=0.
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- First, we solve $\sin{x}=0.$ The solutions to this equation that lie in the given domain are $x = 0^\circ$ and $x=180^\circ.$

- Then, we solve $\cos{x}-\dfrac12=0,$ or equivalently, $\cos{x}=\dfrac12.$ The only solution to this equation that lies in the given domain is $x = 60^\circ.$

Combining all the solutions from both equations, the solutions of the original equation (in ascending order) are

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x,\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta {e}^{-\theta x}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta x}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =5.1+4.2+6.3=15.6\end{aligned}

"Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{10}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼N(\theta ,{1}^{2}),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown mean. For a particular sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{10},$ you're given that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{x}_{i}=41.2,\,{\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{x}_{i}^{2}=182.6.
$$

 
Given that the log-likelihood function of the sample is

$$
l(\theta )=-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )+a+b\theta +c{\theta }^{2},
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$

*Hint: The probability density function for a normal random variable with mean $\theta $ and standard deviation $1$ is given by* 

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=10$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x,\theta )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Next, we write down the log-density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x,\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{(x-\theta )^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2} \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

We are told that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{x}_{i}=41.2,$ ${\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{x}_{i}^{2}=182.6,$ and $n=10.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-\frac{10}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}(182.6-2\theta \cdot 41.2+10{\theta }^{2}) \\  & =-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )+(-91.3)+41.2\theta +(-5){\theta }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b+c=(-91.3)+41.2+(-5)=-55.1.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-689ba3cb-114a-56ff-8abb-81f20075f5f3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-689ba3cb-114a-56ff-8abb-81f20075f5f3" :answer-field/id #uuid "689ba3cb-114a-56ff-8abb-81f20075f5f3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-48337ab4-cd65-553e-b93c-57c20fa8194e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ebf9a326-b0aa-5098-aa51-d8aa62a227d1" "answer-48337ab4-cd65-553e-b93c-57c20fa8194e" "answer-42f17b6e-adee-5418-8a80-24659c92c3a5" "answer-2dbd9de5-ffb6-5a92-af24-1a190f516d4b" "answer-a31bea97-b4ca-5c19-a543-03494bd16286"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ebf9a326-b0aa-5098-aa51-d8aa62a227d1" :answer/id #uuid "ebf9a326-b0aa-5098-aa51-d8aa62a227d1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-51.4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-48337ab4-cd65-553e-b93c-57c20fa8194e" :answer/id #uuid "48337ab4-cd65-553e-b93c-57c20fa8194e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-55.1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-42f17b6e-adee-5418-8a80-24659c92c3a5" :answer/id #uuid "42f17b6e-adee-5418-8a80-24659c92c3a5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-57.3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2dbd9de5-ffb6-5a92-af24-1a190f516d4b" :answer/id #uuid "2dbd9de5-ffb6-5a92-af24-1a190f516d4b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "52.5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a31bea97-b4ca-5c19-a543-03494bd16286" :answer/id #uuid "a31bea97-b4ca-5c19-a543-03494bd16286" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "53.8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-5c4c55fe-2946-5795-a8c6-76c349270710" :question/id #uuid "5c4c55fe-2946-5795-a8c6-76c349270710" :question/math-academy-id "q-159960" :question/problem "Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼N(\theta ,{1}^{2}),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown mean. :question/id #uuid "d9c0d129-478a-533e-ada4-db9e83c26531" :question/math-academy-id "q-67450" :question/problem "Given that $8$, $2x$, and $x$ are the first three terms of a geometric sequence, find $x.$" :question/worked-solution "The first three terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}=8,\,{a}_{2}=2x,\,{a}_{3}=x.\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio of the first two terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{2x}{8}=\frac{x}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the common ratio of the second and third terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{x}{2x}=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the values for $r$ and solving for $x,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{4} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cbcf9c63-b025-5bf8-b0d4-e2ed9ac04b61"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id geometric sequences?

I. $-3,\,33,\,-363,\,…$

II. $4,\,52,\,572,\,…$

III. $-2,\,24,\,-312,\,…$" :question/worked-solution "A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{33}{(-3)}=-11 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-363)}{33}=-11\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{52}{4}=13 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{572}{52}=11\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence III is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{24}{(-2)}=-12 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-312)}{24}=-13\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, only sequence I could be a geometric sequence." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c39a56b0-17ca-5ba8-97f8-8c9ae43975ba"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-c39a56b0-17ca-5ba8-97f8-8c9ae43975ba" :answer-field/id #uuid "c39a56b0-17ca-5ba8-97f8-8c9ae43975ba" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-33cbb00f-07b5-51f0-be9d-4a6856c47b23" :answer-field/choices ["answer-995472d2-4a77-572a-a7b7-711efd1e590b" "answer-33cbb00f-07b5-51f0-be9d-4a6856c47b23" "answer-dd60e458-a551-5764-8eed-77a2db9e815e" "answer-d8403a05-8be0-5213-a984-3ab18c368b94" "answer-560c99d8-6dc4-559c-9c1c-50a616a7568f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-995472d2-4a77-572a-a7b7-711efd1e590b" :answer/id #uuid "995472d2-4a77-572a-a7b7-711efd1e590b" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-33cbb00f-07b5-51f0-be9d-4a6856c47b23" :answer/id #uuid "33cbb00f-07b5-51f0-be9d-4a6856c47b23" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dd60e458-a551-5764-8eed-77a2db9e815e" :answer/id #uuid "dd60e458-a551-5764-8eed-77a2db9e815e" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d8403a05-8be0-5213-a984-3ab18c368b94" :answer/id #uuid "d8403a05-8be0-5213-a984-3ab18c368b94" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-560c99d8-6dc4-559c-9c1c-50a616a7568f" :answer/id #uuid "560c99d8-6dc4-559c-9c1c-50a616a7568f" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-b85423f1-a316-59dd-932f-ac0693226903" :question/id #uuid "b85423f1-a316-59dd-932f-ac0693226903" :question/math-academy-id "q-109800" :question/problem "Which of the sequences below are geometric sequences?

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{64}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =\frac{64}{x} \\ 4x & =64 \\ x & =\frac{64}{4} \\ x & =16.\end{aligned}

:question/worked-solution "Applying the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\cdot {4}^{x}-2{e}^{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\cdot {4}^{x})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{e}^{x}) \\  & =3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({4}^{x})-2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x}) \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)\cdot {4}^{x}-2{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(3\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)\cdot {4}^{x}-2{e}^{x})|}_{x=1} \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)\cdot {4}^{1}-2{e}^{1} \\  & =12\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-2e.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b41aee66-8662-5e0a-8dc7-1405a17238b0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b41aee66-8662-5e0a-8dc7-1405a17238b0" :answer-field/id #uuid "b41aee66-8662-5e0a-8dc7-1405a17238b0" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-8301abdf-6346-54fc-a966-bee78fbb19e6" :answer-field/choices ["answer-8301abdf-6346-54fc-a966-bee78fbb19e6"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8301abdf-6346-54fc-a966-bee78fbb19e6" :answer/id #uuid "8301abdf-6346-54fc-a966-bee78fbb19e6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "12\ln 4-2e" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-0f325821-aed1-5216-b5a3-ffaf528190d5" :question/id #uuid "0f325821-aed1-5216-b5a3-ffaf528190d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-340284" :question/problem "Given that $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-3\cdot {2}^{x}$, the slope of the tangent at $x=1$ is{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Applying the formula, we get

"Given the singular value decomposition $A=UΣ{V}^{T},$ where $A$ is a $4\times 2$ matrix, which of the following statements are true?

I. $U$ is a $4\times 4$ orthogonal matrix

II. $Σ$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix

III. $V$ is a diagonal matrix with only positive elements on the main diagonal" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of an $m\times n$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $m\times n$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $m\times m$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $n\times n$ matrix.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $4\times 2$ matrix, $U$ in the singular value decomposition $UΣ{V}^{T}$ must be a $4\times 4$ orthogonal matrix.

- Statement II is false. Since $A$ is a $4\times 2$ matrix, $Σ$ must be a $4\times 2$ matrix.

- Statement III is false. The matrix $V$ in the singular value decomposition $UΣ{V}^{T}$ must be an orthogonal matrix, not a diagonal matrix.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9d2a03a5-a99e-5c9a-aa6c-8403dc252051"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-9d2a03a5-a99e-5c9a-aa6c-8403dc252051" :answer-field/id #uuid "9d2a03a5-a99e-5c9a-aa6c-8403dc252051" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-87a762ea-1f1b-52db-9e42-9df82522b93d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4ee1bbdc-7319-50f5-b95b-e0b9229082a0" "answer-87a762ea-1f1b-52db-9e42-9df82522b93d" "answer-75c1a5b8-85c2-5eb5-b5b9-c7bab8ab41a0" "answer-5d4fe57c-b619-5bf4-a435-2a7ba27bfb30" "answer-4590f3bd-e752-5e65-a452-9b1d195950f1"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4ee1bbdc-7319-50f5-b95b-e0b9229082a0" :answer/id #uuid "4ee1bbdc-7319-50f5-b95b-e0b9229082a0" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-87a762ea-1f1b-52db-9e42-9df82522b93d" :answer/id #uuid "87a762ea-1f1b-52db-9e42-9df82522b93d" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-75c1a5b8-85c2-5eb5-b5b9-c7bab8ab41a0" :answer/id #uuid "75c1a5b8-85c2-5eb5-b5b9-c7bab8ab41a0" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5d4fe57c-b619-5bf4-a435-2a7ba27bfb30" :answer/id #uuid "5d4fe57c-b619-5bf4-a435-2a7ba27bfb30" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4590f3bd-e752-5e65-a452-9b1d195950f1" :answer/id #uuid "4590f3bd-e752-5e65-a452-9b1d195950f1" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162664 :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}{v}_{11} & {v}_{12} \\ {v}_{21} & {v}_{22}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the value of $|{v}_{12}|+|{v}_{22}|?$" :question/worked-solution "If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ the columns of $V$ must be the right singular vectors of $A,$ i.e., the unit eigenvectors of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that the singular values are ${\sigma }_{1}=3$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=2.$ So, the second column of $V$ corresponds to the singular value ${\sigma }_{2}=2.$

Hence, we need to find a unit eigenvector of ${A}^{T}\,A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=4.$ 

- Computing ${A}^{T}\,A,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Computing ${A}^{T}\,A-4I,$ we get

$$
{A}^{T}\,A-4I=[\begin{aligned}8 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

- Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-4I)v=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we get 

$$
\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore,

$$
|{v}_{12}|+|{v}_{22}|=|\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}|+|\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}|=\frac{3}{\sqrt{5}}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186161276 :answer-field/correct 17592186161278 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163247 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix, and 

$$
A= U\Sigma V^T
$$

is a singular value decomposition of $A.$ Let's describe how to find the matrices $V$ and $\Sigma$ of this singular value decomposition. 

Notice that if we compute $A^TA,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={(UΣ{V}^{T})}^{T}(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =(V{Σ}^{T}\,{U}^{T})(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =V{Σ}^{T}({U}^{T}\,U)Σ{V}^{T} \\  & =V{Σ}^{T}({I}_{n})Σ{V}^{T} \\  & =V({Σ}^{T}\,Σ){V}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

From here, we note that $A^T \! A$ is always symmetric, and that $\Sigma^T \! \Sigma$ is a diagonal matrix with the squares of the singular values on the main diagonal. As a result,

$$
A^TA = V\left( \Sigma^T \Sigma\right) V^T
$$

is an orthogonal diagonalization of the symmetric matrix $A^T \! A.$ So, to find the matrix $V$ in our SVD, we need to orthogonally diagonalize $A^T A.$

Let's demonstrate how this works in practice by computing the matrices $\Sigma$ and $V$ in the SVD of the matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/b7/b766ec7d8c00dfc121e707566d21db470c087c3e785f4e1b2868e7f932873c67.svg)

We proceed as follows:

- Computing $A^T \! A,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ -6 & 13\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Solving the characteristic equation $|A^T \! A - \lambda I| = 0,$ we get the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A \mathbin{:}$

$$
{\color{blue}{\lambda_1 = 16}}, \qquad  {\color{red}{\lambda_2 = 1}}
$$

So, the corresponding singular values are 

$$
{\color{blue}\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}  = 4},  \qquad {\color{red}\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2} = 1}.
$$

We now find a unit eigenvector basis of $A^T \! A.$ These unit eigenvectors will be the columns of our matrix $V$ in the orthogonal diagonalization of $A^T \! A$.

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1).
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=5t,\,{p}_{2}(t)=-2t+2,\,q(t)=-t-4
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ given that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1}(t)\}$ equals $-5t.$" :question/worked-solution "Since the set $\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,q(t)={\text{proj}}_{{p}_{1}(t)}\,q(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{2}(t)}\,q(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{p}_{1}(t)}\,q(t)=-5t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{p}_{2}(t)\}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{2}(t)}\,q(t)=\frac{⟨q(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{p}_{2}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨q(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & =q(0){p}_{2}(0)+q(1){p}_{2}(1) \\  & =(-t-4){|}_{0}\cdot (-2t+2){|}_{0}+(-t-4){|}_{1}\cdot (-2t+2){|}_{1} \\  & =(-4)\cdot 2+(-5)\cdot 0 \\  & =-8,\end{aligned}
$$

  

and

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={p}_{2}(0){p}_{2}(0)+{p}_{2}(1){p}_{2}(1) \\  & =(-2t+2)^{2}{|}_{0}+(-2t+2)^{2}{|}_{1} \\  & ={2}^{2}+{0}^{2} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{2}(t)}\,q(t) & =\frac{-8}{4}\cdot (-2t+2)=4t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,q(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{p}_{1}(t)}\,q(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{2}(t)}\,q(t) \\  & =-5t+(4t-4) \\  & =-t-4.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134064 :question/problem "Let $V=C[-\pi ,\pi ],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,g(t)={sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{2}(t)\}$ equals $-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$" :question/worked-solution "Since the set $\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t)\}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{1}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(t){f}_{1}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is an odd function, while ${sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is even. Hence, their product $\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{0}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t=0.
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =0-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133875 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-bb47ff23-1630-5500-b6a4-5200379ffde8"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-bb47ff23-1630-5500-b6a4-5200379ffde8" :question/id #uuid "bb47ff23-1630-5500-b6a4-5200379ffde8" :question/math-academy-id "q-105467" :question/problem "Let $V={R}_{1}[t],$ the vector space of polynomials of degree at most $1$ with real coefficients. $$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{g(t)}\,f(t) & =\frac{⟨f(t),g(t)⟩}{⟨g(t),g(t)⟩}\,g(t) \\  & =\frac{{\int }_{0}^{1}8t\cdot (4t-2)\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{0}^{1}(4t-2)^{2}\,\text{d}t}\cdot (4t-2) \\  & =\frac{{\int }_{0}^{1}(32{t}^{2}-16t)\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{0}^{1}(16{t}^{2}-16t+4)\,\text{d}t}\cdot (4t-2) \\  & =\frac{[\frac{32}{3}{t}^{3}-8{t}^{2}]_{0}^{1}}{[\frac{16}{3}{t}^{3}-8{t}^{2}+4t]_{0}^{1}}\cdot (4t-2) \\  & =\frac{(\frac{32}{3}-8)-0}{(\frac{16}{3}-4)-0}\cdot (6t-3) \\  & =\frac{(\frac{8}{3})}{(\frac{4}{3})}\cdot (4t+2) \\  & =2\cdot (4t-2) \\  & =8t-4.\end{aligned}

$$

![](images/38/38fcf924a077c207ff66fca76d63333d0f28986432b795c889f22b725faca078.png)

The upper sum $U(f,P)$ is given by

$$
U(f,P)={M}_{11}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{11})+{M}_{21}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{21})+{M}_{12}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{12})+{M}_{22}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{22})
$$

where ${M}_{ij}$ is the *maximum* value of $f$ in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ We pick the *maximum* value of $f$ because we're finding the *upper* sum.

Taking into account the fact that $\text{Area}({R}_{ij})=2$ for all $4$ subregions, the formula for $U(f,P)$ reduces to

$$
\begin{aligned}U(f,P) & =2\cdot {M}_{11}+2\cdot {M}_{21}+2\cdot {M}_{12}+2\cdot {M}_{22} \\  & =2({M}_{11}+{M}_{21}+{M}_{12}+{M}_{22}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that

- $f(x,y)=21-xy$ decreases as $x$ increases, and

- $f(x,y)=21-xy$ decreases as $y$ increases.

![](images/9e/9e1d5a5dcf056f15fdf9e15b4caf3a2f506549ec785c752579bce5b6e12662cb.png)

As a result, the *maximum* value of $f$ in each subregion is attained when we have the *smallest* possible $x$ and the *smallest* possible $y.$ This is the value at the *bottom left corner* of each subregion.

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{11} & =f(2,1)=19 \\ {M}_{21} & =f(3,1)=18 \\ {M}_{12} & =f(2,3)=15 \\ {M}_{22} & =f(3,3)=12\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}U(f,P) & =2(19+18+15+12) \\  & =128.\end{aligned}
