:question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-20\lambda {y}^{′}+100{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,1\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-20\lambda m+100{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-10\lambda )(m-10\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=10\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{10\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{10\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{10\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{10\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =10A\lambda {e}^{10\lambda x}+B{e}^{10\lambda x}+10B\lambda x{e}^{10\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}10A\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }+B{e}^{10\lambda }+10B\lambda {e}^{10\lambda } & =0 \\ 10A\lambda +B+10B\lambda  & =0 \\ (10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{20\lambda }+2B{e}^{20\lambda }+2(10A\lambda {e}^{20\lambda }+B{e}^{20\lambda }+20B\lambda {e}^{20\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(10A\lambda +B+20B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+20A\lambda +2B+40B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+20\lambda )A+(4+40\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+20\lambda )A+4(1+10\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B &=0 \\ (1+20\lambda )A+4(1+10\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}10\lambda  & 1+10\lambda  \\ 1+20\lambda  & 4(1+10\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}10\lambda \cdot 4(1+10\lambda )-(1+10\lambda )(1+20\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )[40\lambda -(1+20\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )[40\lambda -1-20\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )(20\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{10}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{20}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{10}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{10{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{10{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+(1-1)B=0
$$

 
which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{20},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{10{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{10{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{3}{2}B=0\,⇒\,A=-3B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-3B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-3) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $Bx{e}^{-x}\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-3).$"} :step/id #uuid "657eea8d-526f-550d-b00d-4e37eca243c7" Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions $y(0)=0$ and $y(2)+{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-14\lambda m+49{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-7\lambda )(m-7\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{7\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{7\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{7\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{7\lambda x}.
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields

$$
A+B\cdot 0=0
$$

which gives $A=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=Bx{e}^{7\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=B{e}^{7\lambda x}+7B\lambda x{e}^{7\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}2B{e}^{14\lambda }+B{e}^{14\lambda }+14B\lambda {e}^{14\lambda } & =0 \\ 3B{e}^{14\lambda }+14B\lambda {e}^{14\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{14\lambda }+\frac{14}{3}B\lambda {e}^{14\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{14\lambda }(1+\frac{14}{3}\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require $B\ne 0.$ Thus, since ${e}^{14\lambda }>0,$ we must have

$$
\lambda =-\frac{3}{14}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =Bx{e}^{7\lambda x} \\  & =Bx{e}^{-\frac{3}{2}x}.\end{aligned}

"q-338729" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-8\lambda {y}^{′}+16{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,1\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-8\lambda m+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-4\lambda )(m-4\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=4\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{4\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{4\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{4\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{4\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =4A\lambda {e}^{4\lambda x}+B{e}^{4\lambda x}+4B\lambda x{e}^{4\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}4A\lambda {e}^{4\lambda }+B{e}^{4\lambda }+4B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ 4A\lambda +B+4B\lambda  & =0 \\ (4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{8\lambda }+2B{e}^{8\lambda }+2(4A\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }+B{e}^{8\lambda }+8B\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(4A\lambda +B+8B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+8A\lambda +2B+16B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+(4+16\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+4(1+4\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B &=0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+4(1+4\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}4\lambda  & 1+4\lambda  \\ 1+8\lambda  & 4(1+4\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4\lambda \cdot 4(1+4\lambda )-(1+4\lambda )(1+8\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )[16\lambda -(1+8\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )[16\lambda -1-8\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )(8\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{8}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{4{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{4{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+(1-1)B=0
$$

 
which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{8},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{4{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{4{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{3}{2}B=0\,⇒\,A=-3B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-3B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-3) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $Bx{e}^{-x}\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-3).$"} :step/id #uuid "216f8e14-7c94-5ef7-babd-78281fa1fe2d" $$

$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$" :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields $A=0.$ Thus, we have a nontrivial solution, so $\lambda =0$ is a parameter value corresponding to the eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 4\text{i}\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda x)
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}=-4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda x)+4B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
-4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+4B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $B=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields

$$
-4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda \pi )=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
4\lambda \pi =n\pi 
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{n}{4}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4{\lambda }_{n}x),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "636715cd-0d7e-58bd-89a4-fedf8f61d582" :step/next {:db/id 17592186530569}} {:db/id 17592186530569 :step/content {:db/id 17592186314746 :question/answer-fields :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-20\lambda {y}^{′}+100{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,1\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-20\lambda m+100{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-10\lambda )(m-10\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=10\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{10\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{10\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{10\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{10\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =10A\lambda {e}^{10\lambda x}+B{e}^{10\lambda x}+10B\lambda x{e}^{10\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}10A\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }+B{e}^{10\lambda }+10B\lambda {e}^{10\lambda } & =0 \\ 10A\lambda +B+10B\lambda  & =0 \\ (10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{20\lambda }+2B{e}^{20\lambda }+2(10A\lambda {e}^{20\lambda }+B{e}^{20\lambda }+20B\lambda {e}^{20\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(10A\lambda +B+20B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+20A\lambda +2B+40B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+20\lambda )A+(4+40\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+20\lambda )A+4(1+10\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B &=0 \\ (1+20\lambda )A+4(1+10\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}10\lambda  & 1+10\lambda  \\ 1+20\lambda  & 4(1+10\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}10\lambda \cdot 4(1+10\lambda )-(1+10\lambda )(1+20\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )[40\lambda -(1+20\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )[40\lambda -1-20\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )(20\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{10}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{20}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{10}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{10{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{10{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+(1-1)B=0
$$

 
which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{20},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{10{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{10{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{3}{2}B=0\,⇒\,A=-3B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-3B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-3) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $Bx{e}^{-x}\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-3).$"} :step/id #uuid "657eea8d-526f-550d-b00d-4e37eca243c7" We can do this using the **quotient rule**.

The quotient rule is very similar to the product rule, except that this time we're dealing with the difference of two logarithms rather than the sum.

The quotient rule states that two logarithms which share a common base $\color{blue}n$ satisfy

$$
\log_{\color{blue}n} (a) - \log_{\color{blue}n} (b) = \log_{\color{blue}n}\left(\dfrac a b\right)
$$

So, we can use this rule to rewrite $\log_{\color{blue}3}(4) - \log_{\color{blue}3}(6)$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log_{3} 4 - \log_{3} (6) &= \log_{3} (\frac{4}{6}) \\
&= \log_{3} (\frac{2}{3})
\end{aligned}
$$

The quotient rule works exactly the same for the natural and common logarithms." :tutorial/id #uuid "3ed13d12-2b3d-5700-8a30-aa21719ebea3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2784 :tutorial/title :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to rewrite $\log_3(4) - \log_3(6)$ as a single logarithm. We can do this using the **quotient rule**.

The quotient rule is very similar to the product rule, except that this time we're dealing with the difference of two logarithms rather than the sum.

The quotient rule states that two logarithms which share a common base $\color{blue}n$ satisfy

$$
\log_{\color{blue}n} (a) - \log_{\color{blue}n} (b) = \log_{\color{blue}n}\left(\dfrac a b\right)
$$

So, we can use this rule to rewrite $\log_{\color{blue}3}(4) - \log_{\color{blue}3}(6)$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log_{3} 4 - \log_{3} (6) &= \log_{3} (\frac{4}{6}) \\
&= \log_{3} (\frac{2}{3})
\end{aligned}
$$

The quotient rule works exactly the same for the natural and common logarithms." :tutorial/id #uuid "3ed13d12-2b3d-5700-8a30-aa21719ebea3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2784 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "90d69d32-99d1-5555-bf3e-f80cdaac3054" :step/math-academy-id 14236 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111488}} {:db/id 17592186111878 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to rewrite $\log_3(4) - \log_3(6)$ as a single logarithm. :question/math-academy-id "e-3775" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186092172 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b6d31a25-823d-59b2-897c-61a75b747c01" :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Trigonometric Equation Containing the Cosine Function Transformed by One Operation"}] :question/problem "Consider the equation $\cos{2x} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ for $0\leq x < 2\pi$. If the solutions $x_1, x_2, x_3$ and $x_4$ are written in ascending order, what is the value of $x_2\cdot x_3$?" :question/worked-solution "We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
2x &= \frac{π}{4} + 2nπ, \mid 2x|= \frac{7π}{4} + 2nπ
\end{aligned}
$$

Solving our two equations for $x$ gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix}x &= \frac{π}{8} + nπ & x|= \frac{7π}{8} + nπ \\ x|= \frac{π}{8} + \frac{8nπ}{8} & x|= \frac{7π}{8} + \frac{8nπ}{8} \\ x|= ((8n + 1)π)/(8) & x|= ((8n + 7)π)/(8)\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

We set

$$
n=0, \pm 1, \pm 2,\ldots
$$

until we have generated all solutions in the domain

$$
0 \leq x \lt 2\pi
$$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ and $x=\dfrac{7\pi}{8}$.
- Setting $n=1$ gives $x=\dfrac{9\pi}{8}$ and $x=\dfrac{15\pi}{8}$.

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain

$$
0 \leq x \lt 2\pi
$$

So, the solutions $x_1, x_2, x_3$ and $x_4$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x = \dfrac{\pi}{8}, \, \dfrac{7\pi}{8}, \, \dfrac{9\pi}{8}, \, \dfrac{15\pi}{8}
$$

Finally,

$$
x_2\cdot x_3 = \dfrac{7\pi}{8} \cdot \dfrac{9\pi}{8} = \dfrac{63\pi^2}{64}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186092778 :question/id #uuid "febbe57d-c5b7-5d66-8f65-3b472489e43c" :question/math-academy-id "q-65966"} {:db/id 17592186092779 :question/id #uuid "75a3de01-6d89-5fc1-965c-d39845cdc4cf" :question/math-academy-id "q-65967"} {:db/id 17592186092173 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186091993 :question/id #uuid "d8397378-838b-5fb1-b3e7-b5c341a17e38" :question/math-academy-id "e-3784"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1286cc9b-2080-5541-88e1-d4d2741ea1e5" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186092631 :question/id #uuid "f784918d-e59a-59a6-99e5-595969e2c1d4" :question/math-academy-id "q-20821"} {:db/id 17592186092840 :question/id #uuid "6a233ee0-69e8-582d-99b2-d6052d005716" :question/math-academy-id "q-8421"}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Trigonometric Equation Containing the Cosine Function Transformed by Multiple Operations"} {:db/id 17592186091993 :question/id #uuid "d8397378-838b-5fb1-b3e7-b5c341a17e38" :question/math-academy-id "e-3784" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186092173 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1286cc9b-2080-5541-88e1-d4d2741ea1e5" :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Trigonometric Equation Containing the Cosine Function Transformed by Multiple Operations"}] :question/problem "Solve the equation $-2\sqrt{3}\cos\left(2x+60^\circ\right) - 3 = 0$ for $0^\circ\leq x < 360^\circ$." :question/worked-solution "First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-2\sqrt{3}\cos (2x + 60^{∘}) - 3 &= 0 \\
- 2\sqrt{3}\cos (2x + 60^{∘}) &= 3 \\
\cos (2x + 60^{∘}) &= -\frac{3}{2\sqrt{3}} \\
\cos (2x + 60^{∘}) &= -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

We will find the general solution to the equation and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}
2x + 60^{∘} &= 150^{∘} + n \cdot 360^{∘}, \mid 2x + 60^{∘}|= 210^{∘} + n \cdot 360^{∘}
\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the two equations above for $x$ gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix}2x &= 150^{∘} - 60^{∘} + n \cdot 360^{∘} & 2x|= 210^{∘} - 60^{∘} + n \cdot 360^{∘} \\ 2x|= 90^{∘} + n \cdot 360^{∘} & 2x|= 150^{∘} + n \cdot 360^{∘} \\ x|= 45^{∘} + n \cdot 180^{∘} & x|= 75^{∘} + n \cdot 180^{∘}\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

We set

$$
n=0, \pm 1, \pm 2,\ldots
$$

until we have generated all solutions in the domain

$$
0^\circ \leq x \lt 360^\circ
$$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=45^\circ$ and $x=75^\circ$.
- Setting $n=1$ gives $x=225^\circ$ and $x=255^\circ$.

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain

$$
0^\circ \leq x \lt 360^\circ
$$

So, the solutions $x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x_1 = 45^\circ,\quad x_2 = 75^\circ,\quad x_3 = 225^\circ,\quad x_4= 255^\circ
$$"} {:db/id 17592186092631 :question/id #uuid "f784918d-e59a-59a6-99e5-595969e2c1d4" :question/math-academy-id "q-20821"} {:db/id 17592186092840 :question/id #uuid "6a233ee0-69e8-582d-99b2-d6052d005716" :question/math-academy-id "q-8421"} {:db/id 17592186092174 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186091997 :question/id #uuid "c672314a-e7f7-5f64-9f59-b49698b76b37" :question/math-academy-id "e-3791"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9e880672-e776-5701-8168-730f7012f5b0" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186092839 :question/id #uuid "9d89a6a4-d185-5501-96b3-d3722a86fa1e" :question/math-academy-id "q-8419"} {:db/id 17592186092847 :question/id #uuid "ac12bbbe-2e0d-5071-ad98-4fcc4a951d95" :question/math-academy-id "q-8472"}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Trigonometric Equation Containing a Transformed Cosine Function Under a Modified Domain"} {:db/id 17592186091997 :question/id #uuid "c672314a-e7f7-5f64-9f59-b49698b76b37" :question/math-academy-id "e-3791" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186092174 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9e880672-e776-5701-8168-730f7012f5b0" :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Trigonometric Equation Containing a Transformed Cosine Function Under a Modified Domain"}] :question/problem "Solve the equation $\cos\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $-2\pi < x \leq 0$." :question/worked-solution "We will find the general solution to the equation and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}
2x + \frac{π}{4} &= -\frac{2π}{3} + 2nπ, \mid 2x + \frac{π}{4}|= \frac{2π}{3} + 2nπ
\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the two equations above for $x$ gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix}2x &= -\frac{11π}{12} + 2nπ & 2x|= \frac{5π}{12} + 2nπ \\ x|=-\frac{11π}{24} + nπ & x|= \frac{5π}{24} + nπ \\ x|= ((24n - 11)π)/(24) & x|= ((24n + 5)π)/(24)\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

We set

$$
n=0, \pm 1, \pm 2,\ldots
$$

until we have generated all solutions in the domain

$$
-2\pi < x \leq 0
$$

- Setting $n=-2$ gives $x=-\dfrac{59\pi}{24}$ and $x=-\dfrac{43\pi}{24}$. We reject the solution $-\dfrac{59\pi}{24}$ since it lies outside the domain of interest.
- Setting $n=-1$ gives $x=-\dfrac{35\pi}{24}$ and $x=-\dfrac{19\pi}{24}$.
- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=-\dfrac{11\pi}{24}$ and $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{24}$. We reject the solution $\dfrac{5\pi}{24}$ since it lies outside the domain of interest.

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain

$$
-2\pi < x \leq 0
$$

So, the solutions $x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x_1 = -\dfrac{43\pi}{24}, \quad x_2=-\dfrac{35\pi}{24}, \quad x_3 = -\dfrac{19\pi}{24}, \quad x_4 = -\dfrac{11\pi}{24}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186092839 :question/id #uuid "9d89a6a4-d185-5501-96b3-d3722a86fa1e" :question/math-academy-id "q-8419"} {:db/id 17592186092847 :question/id #uuid "ac12bbbe-2e0d-5071-ad98-4fcc4a951d95" :question/math-academy-id "q-8472"} {:db/id 17592186050080} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186092973} :activity/id #uuid "81af9a68-b130-5677-9448-07c433454ec2" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048625 :topic/id #uuid "af9f4926-ffe7-585c-be25-f4e24467b430" :topic/math-academy-id 921} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186092973 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093391 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find all of the solutions to

$$
\cos\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}, \qquad -\pi \leq x < \pi
$$

Notice that the equation contains a transformed cosine function.

We know that the general solution to the elementary equation

$$
\cos{X} = \dfrac{1}{2}
$$

is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
X &= \frac{π}{3} + 2nπ, \mid X|= \frac{5π}{3} + 2nπ
\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is assumed to be any integer.

To find the general solution of the transformed cosine equation, we replace $X$ with the input of the cosine function, which is

$$
x + \dfrac{\pi}{3}
$$

in this case. This gives the general solution

$$
x+\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{3} + 2n\pi, \qquad\qquad x+\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}+ 2n\pi
$$

We now solve the above two equations for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= 2nπ \mid x|= \frac{4π}{3} + 2nπ \\
x &= \frac{4π}{3} + \frac{6nπ}{3} \\
x &= (2π(2 + 3n))/(3)
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set

$$
n = 0, \pm1, \pm2, \ldots
$$

until we have generated all solutions in the domain

$$
-\pi \leq x < \pi
$$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$. We reject the solution $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ since it lies outside the domain of interest.
- Setting $n=-1$ gives $x=-2\pi$ and $x=-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$. We reject the solution $-2\pi$ since it lies outside the domain of interest.

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain

$$
-\pi \leq x < \pi
$$

So, the solutions $x_1$ and $x_2$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x_1 = -\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\qquad x_2 = 0
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ca38e435-6d4e-550b-83d2-62b4e80d4eda" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2684 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "724852af-67e5-54bd-91c0-766dd3dabaf7" :step/math-academy-id Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186092424} {:db/id 17592186092973 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093391 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find all of the solutions to

$$
\cos\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}, \qquad -\pi \leq x < \pi
$$

Notice that the equation contains a transformed cosine function.

We know that the general solution to the elementary equation

$$
\cos{X} = \dfrac{1}{2}
$$

is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
X &= \frac{π}{3} + 2nπ, \mid X|= \frac{5π}{3} + 2nπ
\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is assumed to be any integer.

To find the general solution of the transformed cosine equation, we replace $X$ with the input of the cosine function, which is

$$
x + \dfrac{\pi}{3}
$$

in this case. This gives the general solution

$$
x+\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{3} + 2n\pi, \qquad\qquad x+\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}+ 2n\pi
$$

We now solve the above two equations for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= 2nπ \mid x|= \frac{4π}{3} + 2nπ \\
x &= \frac{4π}{3} + \frac{6nπ}{3} \\
x &= (2π(2 + 3n))/(3)
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set

$$
n = 0, \pm1, \pm2, \ldots
$$

until we have generated all solutions in the domain

$$
-\pi \leq x < \pi
$$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$. We reject the solution $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ since it lies outside the domain of interest.
- Setting $n=-1$ gives $x=-2\pi$ and $x=-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$. We reject the solution $-2\pi$ since it lies outside the domain of interest.

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain

$$
-\pi \leq x < \pi
$$

So, the solutions $x_1$ and $x_2$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x_1 = -\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\qquad x_2 = 0
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ca38e435-6d4e-550b-83d2-62b4e80d4eda" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2684 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "724852af-67e5-54bd-91c0-766dd3dabaf7" :step/math-academy-id 13025 :step/next {:db/id 17592186092974}} {:db/id 17592186093391 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find all of the solutions to

:topic/math-academy-id 3595} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186176826 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177047 :tutorial/content "Given a dataset of paired numerical observations $(x,y)$ and the corresponding linear regression model

$$
\widehat{y} =f(x)
$$

the **residual** for a particular observation $(x, y)$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}
Residual &= Actual - Estimated \\
&= y - f(x) \\
&= y - y^(^)
\end{aligned}
$$

We subtract the *estimated* value predicted by the model from the actual *observed* value.

To illustrate this concept graphically, consider the following example.

The owner of an ice cream shop keeps track of the average daily temperature $x$ (measured in $^\circ \mathrm{F}$) and the resulting daily ice cream sales $y$ (in dollars). The scatter plot for several randomly selected days and the corresponding linear regression line are shown below.

Suppose the equation of the regression line is

$$
y= 2.5 x +165
$$

Let's use our regression line to compute the residual of the point with coordinates $\color{red}(82, 360)$ (shown in red on our graph).

First, notice that since the highlighted data point has coordinates ${\color{red}(82, 360)}$, our actual value is

$$
y = {\color{red}360}
$$

Next, we compute the predicted value using our linear regression model:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^(^) &= 2.5x + 165 \\
&= 2.5(82) + 165 \\
&= 370
\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/38/3843c71b50251ae035378507ffb22cfade48dff8e1544d8e1317e4e6d611f7a1.png)

Finally, we compute the residual:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Residual &= Actual - Estimated \\
&= y - y^(^) \\
&= 360 - 370 \\
&=-10
\end{aligned}
$$

$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2\},$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=1\cdot 2=2.$ 

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{2}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{[\frac{1}{3}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{M}{2}(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{8}{3}) \\  & =\frac{M}{2}\cdot \frac{10}{3} \\  & =\frac{5M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia is $\frac{5M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186129532 :question/id #uuid "f0af98bb-12cf-5c0f-a924-a0fe039adf99" :question/math-academy-id "q-162906"} {:db/id 17592186281631 :question/id #uuid "f8b4a4d7-db6d-5f9c-bc7b-f800dc788f58" :question/math-academy-id "q-163200"} {:db/id 17592186281632 :question/id #uuid "4167aa80-a0c6-5dcf-ad5c-868018ed4d84" :question/math-academy-id "q-163201" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "35a4e499-61e4-5d51-8488-e60716c8b89c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279063} {:answer/id #uuid "4dc2f52c-6937-5664-b1ad-a8e9f01fba53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6M\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279296} {:answer/id #uuid "77349270-7aa3-5ac9-a411-62c1c99df8b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3M\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279656} {:answer/id #uuid "81467cbe-f5a5-5724-8a67-a32eb23c17bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3M}{2}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279753} {:answer/id #uuid "e207c367-c309-58d1-92c5-7517420bb1d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2M\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280589}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279656} :answer-field/id #uuid "5beaea88-1fc4-552a-a4a5-3b0f75db282a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186280991}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 3=6.$ 

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{x},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}[x]_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{[\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{9}\cdot 27 \\  & =3M.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{4}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{y},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{8}{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{[\frac{8y}{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{2M}{3}(3-1) \\  & =\frac{4M}{3}.\end{aligned}

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type II region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,\frac{y}{3}\le x\le 4-y\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/47/47c897bd58a23965d9c36f683553c0817afa8bc2e37ed53a432edcd62b386e55.png)

The area of the triangular plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot 3=6.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{y/3}^{4-y}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}[{\int }_{y/3}^{4-y}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}(4-y-\frac{1}{3}y)\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{y}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{[\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{3}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{6}(36-27) \\  & =\frac{3M}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281637 :question/id #uuid "9a1f6eeb-74ef-55ae-8480-c174f3bc8d34" :question/math-academy-id "q-163219" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129211 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "92cc3d27-0e31-571f-9b92-4f209c5a08e0" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Moment of Inertia of a Lamina With Uniform Mass Density"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "839f5ece-276f-5816-96b9-c527a2493a8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2M}{3}" :db/id 17592186279770} {:answer/id #uuid "b9e6e3da-9c21-52c4-86e6-90e111164bf1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3M}{4}" :db/id 17592186280230} {:answer/id #uuid "d898035f-95c6-5b96-a44f-c85c5e0fb62a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{M}{3}" :db/id 17592186280506} {:answer/id #uuid "f28d76a8-28fa-5a01-aefa-cb1bdd261513" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2M" :db/id 17592186280703} {:answer/id #uuid "ffd690e9-c999-5620-b45c-5474e864788b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3M" :db/id 17592186280831}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "839f5ece-276f-5816-96b9-c527a2493a8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2M}{3}" :db/id 17592186279770} :answer-field/id #uuid "faab536c-ba69-524a-89bb-9d4a9ee45c2f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186281279}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/c6/c683f411b11b7b353e166364c8e0fdbc0d218c07535c2f3430d832ab129702d8.png)

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,\frac{x}{2}\le y\le 3-x\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/6c/6c2cec5e919c25623396b5ba5f052481623a868c7520aa8e3d1d3eb34f3a4a58.png)

The area of the triangular plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 3=3.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x/2}^{3-x}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}[{\int }_{x/2}^{3-x}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}(3-x-\frac{x}{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}3{x}^{2}-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{[{x}^{3}-\frac{3}{8}{x}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{M}{3}(8-6) \\  & =\frac{2M}{3}.\end{aligned}

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type II region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,y\le x\le 2-y\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/b1/b1ced30e4cc1fe984b56707f11e8720f2ee68c5b204b6ea7b8d607a65276acca.png)

The area of the triangular plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 1=1.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=M.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{2-y}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{y}^{2-y}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2-y)^{3}-{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{[-\frac{1}{4}(2-y)^{4}-\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{M}{12}{[(2-y)^{4}+{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{M}{12}(1+1-16-0) \\  & =\frac{7M}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186426168 :question/id #uuid "a005e400-255d-52bf-b2df-866a68951503" :question/math-academy-id "q-163203" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a308805-aad8-54a7-b5b1-064462e81b88" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{22M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186426082} {:answer/id #uuid "383fad8b-59a8-5b43-ad3d-50f07ba39230" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "13\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186426094} {:answer/id #uuid "7cd77a93-c9ac-5031-8c15-eb3b4d405d24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "26M\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186426110} {:answer/id #uuid "b11137df-53c8-5030-b8e0-6a9bb71fdcb0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{16M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186426131} {:answer/id #uuid "f370ad7c-77cf-51a3-8d2a-a9e647d5cb34" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{13M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186426145}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426145} :answer-field/id #uuid "73ed7367-47d9-5ab5-97c8-cd0c7ced1597" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186426153}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=3\cdot 2=6.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{4}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}{y}^{2}[x]_{1}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{[{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{6}(27-1) \\  & =\frac{13M}{3}.\end{aligned}

Find the moment of inertia of this lamina about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(6-xy)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{2}6{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}y+6{y}^{2}-x{y}^{3}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[2{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}y+6x{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}16-4y+12{y}^{2}-2{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[16y-2{y}^{2}+4{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{4}]_{0}^{3} \\  & =48-18+108-\frac{81}{2}-0 \\  & =97.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia of the lamina about the origin is $97.5\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186129534 :question/id #uuid "cea62eec-0c97-53ea-9e5d-d067ab50729f" :question/math-academy-id "q-162924"} {:db/id 17592186235553 :question/id #uuid "869d1799-99c2-550a-99bc-bd6dd9290649" :question/math-academy-id "q-169103"} {:db/id 17592186281611 :question/id #uuid "e73bf43d-4842-564c-b994-8b4ed88b9ee2" :question/math-academy-id "q-163146" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00586df5-9953-5e7a-a58f-2329aa16a468" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186278586} {:answer/id #uuid "3bf84ed5-f917-50b8-8e4d-80368c472356" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279121} {:answer/id #uuid "4237198b-add2-521b-b160-d585a0924755" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279184} {:answer/id #uuid "58055d99-9594-5371-bd9f-20b8d761809d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279400} {:answer/id #uuid "86941ae5-17f0-581b-91b1-2673bcdf9949" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279793}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279121} :answer-field/id #uuid "945c0f7a-70d5-5057-8a4c-71bc5f6f818a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281099}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A rectangular plate occupies the region

$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 4,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x}\},

as shown below.

$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}\},

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(10y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}10{x}^{2}y+10{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[5{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{x}^{2}(4-{x}^{2})+\frac{5}{2}{(4-{x}^{2})}^{2}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5}{2}(4-{x}^{2})(2{x}^{2}+4-{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}16-{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{[16x-\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}(32-\frac{32}{5}) \\  & =64.\end{aligned}

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type II region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,y\le x\le 2-{y}^{2},\,\,0\le y\le 1\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/7a/7a4216a2b1dc3859776c6589459d687981b79b123fa3a5eea638d31529e5cd3a.png)

Using the formula for ${I}_{x},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{2-{y}^{2}}{y}^{2}\cdot 12y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{y}^{2-{y}^{2}}12{y}^{3}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[12x{y}^{3}]_{x=y}^{x=2-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}12(2-{y}^{2}){y}^{3}-12{y}^{4}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}24{y}^{3}-12{y}^{5}-12{y}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[6{y}^{4}-2{y}^{6}-\frac{12}{5}{y}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =6-2-\frac{12}{5} \\  & =\frac{8}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481404 :question/id #uuid "a91e5e5e-7869-5527-a5f1-b8a7012a6c8a" :question/math-academy-id "q-163171" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a9485ad-0d2d-50b4-b908-d8715c6808c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "75\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186480793} {:answer/id #uuid "1b253e13-148e-5e5e-a20a-b5b94224af45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "94.2\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186480795} {:answer/id #uuid "54795f54-0a40-564c-911b-ae120e159861" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "82\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186480891} {:answer/id #uuid "6d69e97d-0fc0-5bb2-b5a3-efd04876068d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "90\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186480945} {:answer/id #uuid "746e5210-a7d2-5781-83fe-86be72c56d8d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "86.4\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186480953}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186480945} :answer-field/id #uuid "362d2433-4c99-52b8-885b-22db14bc5af2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481257}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A rectangular plate occupies the region

17592186281147}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M$ occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2}.$
The mass density at each point is proportional to its distance from the $y$-axis.
Find the moment of inertia of the lamina about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

From the description, the mass density function can be written as

$$
\lambda (x,y)=k|x|=kx,
$$

where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find an expression for $k$ in terms of $M$ by integrating the density function over the plate:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}kx\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =k({\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}y) \\  & =k{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\cdot [y]_{0}^{2} \\  & =k(\frac{1}{2}-0)(2-0) \\  & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=M$ and hence $\lambda (x,y)=kx=Mx.$
Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =M{[\frac{1}{4}y+\frac{1}{6}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =M(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =\frac{11M}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281624 :question/id #uuid "8ba69e53-fc8f-5143-953e-05bbe8878807" :question/math-academy-id "q-163180"} {:db/id 17592186281627 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/82/82ed1d9c8965c445488256f2319bd2e1a25b2f685d5ad39c88f2b2ba7f7f5525.png)

Consider a plate of mass $M$ that occupies the region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9,$ shown above. Given that the mass is distributed uniformly across the plate, find the moment of inertia of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The area of the plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{4}\pi {r}^{2}=\frac{9\pi }{4}.
$$

 

Since the mass is distributed uniformly, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{4M}{9\pi }.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4M}{9\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4M}{9\pi }({\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{4M}{9\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}{|}_{0}^{3}\cdot \theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{4M}{9\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{4}(81-0)\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{9M}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129538 :question/id #uuid "41c034f9-14b4-5bc4-9351-1214f69c2032" :question/math-academy-id "q-162990" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3056ba5d-f7d1-55a3-8c91-5da94f695f90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9-4\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186426091} {:answer/id #uuid "32392a3b-31a7-5a44-8746-b4c85858d143" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5-2\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186426092} {:answer/id #uuid "77d105e7-3ddf-576d-b7fd-6524428a349e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4-2\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186426108} {:answer/id #uuid "7faf887c-1e04-5044-ade7-d44593ea0768" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8-3\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186426111} {:answer/id #uuid "d52f3d90-a693-584a-a56c-1a94156d2638" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10-4\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186426136}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426136} :answer-field/id #uuid "1239f0fe-7d29-5b4f-895a-1d599c74b28e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186126725}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "![](images/0a/0a85b0be5f8e5db2cf4d1716e4afe4a2780c500d94a1ce282a9d0044f93ba084.png)

Consider a plate of mass $M$ that occupies the region $D$ bounded by the polar circles $r=1$ and $r=2,$ as shown above. The mass density at any point is proportional to its distance from the origin. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that the region $D,$ in polar coordinates, can be expressed as

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

From the description, the mass density function can be written as $\lambda (r,\theta )=kr,$ where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find an expression for $k$ in terms of $M$ by integrating the density function over the plate:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}kr\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}k{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =k({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =k\cdot \frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}\,{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =k\cdot \frac{7}{3}\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =\frac{14\pi k}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=kr=\frac{3M}{14\pi }r.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{3M}{14\pi }r\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2}\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}\,{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\theta +\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }\cdot \frac{31}{5}\cdot \pi  \\  & =\frac{93M}{70}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186326720 :question/id #uuid "29252808-04b0-5c9a-8f7e-a13993dbc1ba" :question/math-academy-id "q-38822"} {:db/id 17592186367867 :question/id #uuid "Suppose a massless, rigid lamina rotates with angular velocity $\omega$ about a fixed axis $L.$ Attached to the lamina are a set of particles $P_1,P_2,\ldots,P_n$ of masses $m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n$ at distances $r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_n$ from the axis, respectively. 

![](images/b4/b4eeef756faf65e7caaf5bb8dad8d803cacf3e4f17b719868b647bf7e9c9da89.png)

Let's find the total kinetic energy of this system.

Each particle $P_i$ of mass $m_i$ has linear speed $v_i = r_i\omega.$ So, its kinetic energy is

$$
\dfrac12m_iv_i^2 = \dfrac12m_i(r_i\omega)^2 = \dfrac12m_ir_i^2\omega^2.
$$

The total kinetic energy of the system is obtained by adding the energies of all the particles. So, the kinetic energy of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total KE} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{2}{m}_{i}{r}_{i}^{2}{\omega }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i}{r}_{i}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the total kinetic energy of the system is given by 

$$
\text{Total KE} = \dfrac12I\omega^2,
$$

where the quantity

$$
I = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n m_ir_i^2
$$

is called the **moment of inertia** of the system about the fixed axis $L.$ The units of moment of inertia are $\rm{kg}\cdot\rm{m}^2.$

The moment of inertia in angular motion is analogous to mass in linear motion:

- For linear motion, the kinetic energy is given by

$$
\text{KE} = \dfrac12 \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{M} v^2,
$$

where $M$ is the (total) mass of a system of particles.

The mass of a body measures how resistant the body is to changes in linear motion. It takes a larger force to induce a fixed change in linear motion for a large mass than for a smaller mass.

- For angular motion, the kinetic energy is given by

$$
\text{KE} = \dfrac12 \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{I} \omega^2,
$$

where $I$ is the moment of inertia of a system of particles.

The moment of inertia of a body measures how resistant the body is to changes in *angular* motion. It takes a larger force to induce a fixed change in angular motion for an object with a large moment of inertia than for a body with a smaller moment of inertia." :tutorial/id #uuid Consider a plane lamina that occupies the region $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with mass density function $\lambda(x,y),$ (in mass/area), which depends on the position.

By choosing a finite number of points $(x_{ij},y_{ij}),$ where $i=1,2,\ldots,m$ and $j=1,2,\ldots,n,$ we can break the region $D$ into non-overlapping boxes $B_{ij} = [x_{ij}, x_{ij} + \Delta x] \times [y_{ij}, y_{ij} + \Delta y]$ of area $\Delta x \Delta y = \Delta A.$

![](images/c5/c5ac4166ed637b4de525f069673cc6abfaeb2e8e659b3a212d6f2f4d1bf9fc11.png)

For large $m$ and $n,$ the mass density in each box, $B_{ij}$ is approximately constant and equal to the mass density of a point $(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*)$ in the box. Hence, the mass of this part of the lamina is approximately the product of the mass density at this point and the area of the box:

$$
m_{ij} \approx \lambda(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*) \cdot \Delta A
$$

Suppose the function $r(x,y)$ gives the distance of each point $(x,y) \in D$ from a fixed axis $L.$ Then, using the formula for the moment of inertia for a collection of masses, summing over these points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{m}_{i}[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2} \\  & ≈{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(\lambda ({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})\cdot ΔA)[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2} \\  & ≈{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}\lambda ({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2}ΔA.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the limit as the length and width of the boxes tend to zero, we get an exact representation of the moment of inertia as an integral:

$$
I = \lim\limits_{m,n\to \infty} \sum\limits_{i=1}^m \sum\limits_{j=1}^n \lambda(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*) [r(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*)]^2 \Delta A
= \iint\limits_D \lambda(x,y) [r(x,y)]^2 \:\textrm{d}A.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about a fixed axis $L$ of a plane lamina occupying the region $D$ with mass density $\lambda(x,y)$ is

$$
I_L = \iint\limits_D \lambda(x,y) [r(x,y)]^2 \:\textrm{d}A,
$$

where $r(x,y)$ is the distance from the point $(x,y)$ to the axis $L.$

In this lesson, we'll limit the axis of rotation to the $x$- and $y$-axes. Note that the distance between a point $(x,y)$ and the $x$ and $y$ coordinate axes are $r_x(x,y) = |y|$ and $r_y(x,y) = |x|,$ respectively.

![](images/8a/8a94fcdb8bb1a97e2bc9122e88ca7bd4f441299d2ce3c7bee819e644cf4eae89.png)

Hence, the moments of inertia of a plate with respect to the coordinate axes $x$ and $y,$ denoted $I_x$ and $I_y$, respectively, are 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\ {I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

A related concept is the **moment of inertia about the origin** (or **polar moment of inertia**), which deals with the strength of an object when it is rotating. It is defined as

$$
I_0 = \iint\limits_D (x^2+y^2)\lambda(x,y) \:\textrm dA = I_x + I_y.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "170c6cfe-d50a-5cee-b724-5409ca4c8461" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7794 :tutorial/title "Moment of Inertia of Plane Laminas"} :step/id #uuid "3f899894-d69b-5df5-8333-4e2b804563ee" :step/math-academy-id 45104 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130107}}] :activity/title "Moments of Inertia of Laminas About the Coordinate Axes" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186129369} {:db/id 17592186130105 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130411 :tutorial/content "Suppose a massless, rigid lamina rotates with angular velocity $\omega$ about a fixed axis $L.$ Attached to the lamina are a set of particles $P_1,P_2,\ldots,P_n$ of masses $m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n$ at distances $r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_n$ from the axis, respectively. 

![](images/b4/b4eeef756faf65e7caaf5bb8dad8d803cacf3e4f17b719868b647bf7e9c9da89.png)

Let's find the total kinetic energy of this system.

Each particle $P_i$ of mass $m_i$ has linear speed $v_i = r_i\omega.$ So, its kinetic energy is

$$
\dfrac12m_iv_i^2 = \dfrac12m_i(r_i\omega)^2 = \dfrac12m_ir_i^2\omega^2.
$$

The total kinetic energy of the system is obtained by adding the energies of all the particles. So, the kinetic energy of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total KE} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{2}{m}_{i}{r}_{i}^{2}{\omega }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i}{r}_{i}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the total kinetic energy of the system is given by 

$$
\text{Total KE} = \dfrac12I\omega^2,
$$

where the quantity

$$
I = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n m_ir_i^2
$$

is called the **moment of inertia** of the system about the fixed axis $L.$ The units of moment of inertia are $\rm{kg}\cdot\rm{m}^2.$

The moment of inertia in angular motion is analogous to mass in linear motion:

- For linear motion, the kinetic energy is given by

$$
\text{KE} = \dfrac12 \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{M} v^2,
$$

where $M$ is the (total) mass of a system of particles.

The mass of a body measures how resistant the body is to changes in linear motion. It takes a larger force to induce a fixed change in linear motion for a large mass than for a smaller mass.

- For angular motion, the kinetic energy is given by

$$
\text{KE} = \dfrac12 \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{I} \omega^2,
$$

where $I$ is the moment of inertia of a system of particles.

The moment of inertia of a body measures how resistant the body is to changes in *angular* motion. It takes a larger force to induce a fixed change in angular motion for an object with a large moment of inertia than for a body with a smaller moment of inertia." :tutorial/id #uuid "8d36ccdb-eb7d-55de-80e6-f75752dae9db" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5071 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3933d4e7-a615-5065-8581-94f59b08025e" :step/math-academy-id 31761 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130252}} {:db/id 17592186130411 :tutorial/content "Suppose a massless, rigid lamina rotates with angular velocity $\omega$ about a fixed axis $L.$ Attached to the lamina are a set of particles $P_1,P_2,\ldots,P_n$ of masses $m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n$ at distances $r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_n$ from the axis, respectively.

![](images/17/17efc2618db89a57e67423004eba2485ca6af8cd9f71fa271f9540cd0e3c8d74.svg)

- The moment of inertia of ![](images/59/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75ca1d00a5dc4e294d2a8f10fe384d2b2ebf2af38e.svg) about origin is given by

![](images/8f/8f79b08c632cff0162fb8f4c962d44c105e34eb32e8a11cf4eca3868e0362738.svg)

Note that we denote ![](images/10/10b9e6b5ce99ae6bfc544d9480ac6d62cfa9d1f23f78b8b3a331c6c517e1472d.svg) the density function expressed in polar coordinates." :tutorial/id #uuid "5d1a8a74-d440-56ad-b42b-a46e22861e20" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7766 :tutorial/title "Moments of Inertia in Polar Coordinates"} {:db/id 17592186130474 :tutorial/content "Let's now find a formula for the moment of inertia of a plane lamina with continuously varying mass density.

Consider a plane lamina that occupies the region $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with mass density function $\lambda(x,y),$ (in mass/area), which depends on the position.

By choosing a finite number of points $(x_{ij},y_{ij}),$ where $i=1,2,\ldots,m$ and $j=1,2,\ldots,n,$ we can break the region $D$ into non-overlapping boxes $B_{ij} = [x_{ij}, x_{ij} + \Delta x] \times [y_{ij}, y_{ij} + \Delta y]$ of area $\Delta x \Delta y = \Delta A.$

![](images/c5/c5ac4166ed637b4de525f069673cc6abfaeb2e8e659b3a212d6f2f4d1bf9fc11.png)

For large $m$ and $n,$ the mass density in each box, $B_{ij}$ is approximately constant and equal to the mass density of a point $(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*)$ in the box. Hence, the mass of this part of the lamina is approximately the product of the mass density at this point and the area of the box:

$$
m_{ij} \approx \lambda(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*) \cdot \Delta A
$$

Suppose the function $r(x,y)$ gives the distance of each point $(x,y) \in D$ from a fixed axis $L.$ Then, using the formula for the moment of inertia for a collection of masses, summing over these points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{m}_{i}[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2} \\  & ≈{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(\lambda ({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})\cdot ΔA)[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2} \\  & ≈{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}\lambda ({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2}ΔA.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the limit as the length and width of the boxes tend to zero, we get an exact representation of the moment of inertia as an integral:

$$
I = \lim\limits_{m,n\to \infty} \sum\limits_{i=1}^m \sum\limits_{j=1}^n \lambda(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*) [r(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*)]^2 \Delta A
= \iint\limits_D \lambda(x,y) [r(x,y)]^2 \:\textrm{d}A.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about a fixed axis $L$ of a plane lamina occupying the region $D$ with mass density $\lambda(x,y)$ is

$$
I_L = \iint\limits_D \lambda(x,y) [r(x,y)]^2 \:\textrm{d}A,
$$

where $r(x,y)$ is the distance from the point $(x,y)$ to the axis $L.$

In this lesson, we'll limit the axis of rotation to the $x$- and $y$-axes. Note that the distance between a point $(x,y)$ and the $x$ and $y$ coordinate axes are $r_x(x,y) = |y|$ and $r_y(x,y) = |x|,$ respectively.

![](images/8a/8a94fcdb8bb1a97e2bc9122e88ca7bd4f441299d2ce3c7bee819e644cf4eae89.png)

Hence, the moments of inertia of a plate with respect to the coordinate axes $x$ and $y,$ denoted $I_x$ and $I_y$, respectively, are 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\ {I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

A related concept is the **moment of inertia about the origin** (or **polar moment of inertia**), which deals with the strength of an object when it is rotating. It is defined as

$$
I_0 = \iint\limits_D (x^2+y^2)\lambda(x,y) \:\textrm dA = I_x + I_y.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "170c6cfe-d50a-5cee-b724-5409ca4c8461" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7794 :tutorial/title "Moment of Inertia of Plane Laminas"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046660} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186435187} :activity/id #uuid "a8a272ef-3322-59e4-8457-62cd9dcd43be" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049331 :topic/id #uuid "ec6fdbaa-c722-5e5b-b092-5ba93bdf0c02" :topic/math-academy-id 2027} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186435185 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281611 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00586df5-9953-5e7a-a58f-2329aa16a468" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186278586} {:answer/id #uuid "3bf84ed5-f917-50b8-8e4d-80368c472356" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279121} {:answer/id #uuid "4237198b-add2-521b-b160-d585a0924755" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279184} {:answer/id #uuid "58055d99-9594-5371-bd9f-20b8d761809d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279400} {:answer/id #uuid "86941ae5-17f0-581b-91b1-2673bcdf9949" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279793}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279121} :answer-field/id #uuid "945c0f7a-70d5-5057-8a4c-71bc5f6f818a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281099}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e73bf43d-4842-564c-b994-8b4ed88b9ee2" :question/math-academy-id "q-163146" :question/problem "A rectangular plate occupies the region

The mass density function of the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=10x.$ Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=10r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type II region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,y\le x\le 2-{y}^{2},\,\,0\le y\le 1\},

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=10r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{1}^{2}10r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{1}^{2}10{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{2}10{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =2{r}^{5}\,{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =2(32-1)(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-0) \\  & =31\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
