A plate occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the $x$-axis, $y$-axis, and the curve $y=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}$ in the first quadrant, as shown above. If the mass density function of $D$ is given by $\lambda (x,y)=10y,$ find the moment of inertia of the lamina about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/62/626cbf8e182d9eebb8b48026f07c5dd012c1096cc9568465f3648710ea0d07a4.png)

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(10y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}10{x}^{2}y+10{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[5{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{x}^{2}(4-{x}^{2})+\frac{5}{2}{(4-{x}^{2})}^{2}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5}{2}(4-{x}^{2})(2{x}^{2}+4-{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}16-{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{[16x-\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}(32-\frac{32}{5}) \\  & =64.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8cc8c4c3-672d-51c1-af40-2419b51ec4f9" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442861}} {:db/id 17592186442858 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281633 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4c84deba-cb38-5f3b-af0e-58521ec502a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279280} {:answer/id #uuid "a25defa0-44b9-5bda-a10f-e6ef6a677aaa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{16M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280035} {:answer/id #uuid "ad5bf3b6-9c4b-50ce-879e-8ec79739fdf2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280127} {:answer/id #uuid "ca352098-298f-5e14-a7d7-0c7272084e0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8M\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280364} {:answer/id #uuid "cf1d4484-aff6-5376-8a09-a8cd9f6af638" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4M\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280418}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186280127} :answer-field/id #uuid "8a384dc8-494e-5973-bebc-5b4d13e8a8c2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281085}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "095d8c09-ff9b-5528-8c3d-3967d18698a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-163204" :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,1\le y\le 3\},$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 2=4.$ 

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{4}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{y},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{8}{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{[\frac{8y}{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{2M}{3}(3-1) \\  & =\frac{4M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia is $\frac{4M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$"} :step/id #uuid "9a68fb24-0279-5aa2-9378-bef9856a349d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442859}} {:db/id 17592186442859 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281642 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17226919-ce93-5049-994f-31d7cd5c10fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7\pi }{6}" :db/id 17592186278798} {:answer/id #uuid "6d3b17cc-de83-57bb-914f-013137289a03" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5\pi }{12}" :db/id 17592186279586} {:answer/id #uuid "78cff65f-0d69-5e60-9e1c-47253821dc1b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{8}" :db/id 17592186279669} {:answer/id #uuid "8d83c82c-bb2f-532f-ab7d-a58f6e2cc4be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186279853} {:answer/id #uuid "e875a915-69ff-5a94-9c30-f7fd03b5fb84" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7\pi }{10}" :db/id 17592186280639}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279586} :answer-field/id #uuid "bf0fe541-fc86-58e2-a9d5-645ba6b20816" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281172}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "2726afac-54d3-5734-a6e0-8fa5ce77d367" :question/math-academy-id "q-163228" :question/problem "![](images/04/044395de3b30755d0c83d489709c38420827f6984af740bc56a3dc5bfaa33794.png)

$$

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,2\le r\le 3,\,\,\frac{\pi }{3}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{1}{{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{2}^{3}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{2}^{3}r\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\,{|}_{2}^{3}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(9-4)\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 5\cdot \frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{12}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c51d9491-b808-5d51-8650-1109d5229668"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17226919-ce93-5049-994f-31d7cd5c10fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value $$

$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{y},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\int }_{2}^{4}{x}^{2}\cdot x{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}[{\int }_{2}^{4}{x}^{3}{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{e}^{2y}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}]}_{2}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}60{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[30{e}^{2y}]_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =120-30 \\  & =90.\end{aligned}

Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type II region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,\frac{y}{3}\le x\le 4-y\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/47/47c897bd58a23965d9c36f683553c0817afa8bc2e37ed53a432edcd62b386e55.png)

The area of the triangular plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot 3=6.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{y/3}^{4-y}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}[{\int }_{y/3}^{4-y}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}(4-y-\frac{1}{3}y)\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{y}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{[\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{3}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{6}(36-27) \\  & =\frac{3M}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "63d1ac8f-1120-57bf-a3f2-068394de0e68" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481469}} {:db/id 17592186481456 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281644 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24eeb6dc-6a62-5d90-a207-0acfc7258433" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186278919} {:answer/id #uuid "349f0582-d339-5e4d-9545-b31c93cda4da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{2}-1" :db/id 17592186279045} {:answer/id #uuid "538264a8-2746-5c22-950d-ad36b0c19129" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{2}-1}{8}" :db/id 17592186279351} {:answer/id #uuid "c7b8065a-0247-55f8-99df-fad5f0147068" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186280342} {:answer/id #uuid "f2ebd0da-d30a-58a4-863a-0db44212f7d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}" :db/id 17592186280710}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279351} :answer-field/id #uuid "ec2db863-9898-51d6-ba39-8b881e966e18" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281253}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b6b312d9-6efa-541f-ad5d-be93b575260c" :question/math-academy-id "q-163230" :question/problem "![](images/ad/ad7c939aded3f5e5e1e2f3b5e5743609e331625479c25f6a55659be730ed1cf5.png)

The mass density function of the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=15y.$ Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le \sqrt[5]{2},\,\,\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=15r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}15r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}15{r}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}5{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & ={r}^{5}\,{|}_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}\cdot (-{cos}^{3}⁡\theta )\,{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3} \\  & =(2-1)\cdot (-\frac{1}{8}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}) \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}-1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6cb00066-5889-5430-a707-e706993fe08c"} {:db/id 17592186481462 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281622 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1e774e3e-5483-570a-be90-3556fdfeef80" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "96" :db/id 17592186278875} {:answer/id #uuid "264c43c5-9ce5-5021-829e-191395085650" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "66" :db/id 17592186278931} {:answer/id #uuid "27a3b396-361a-5015-9461-0aae23b48259" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "88" :db/id 17592186278947} {:answer/id #uuid "4373458f-0c28-5ba9-9faf-49c7a51e957d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "124" :db/id 17592186279197} {:answer/id #uuid "aec868ad-08a2-517d-b508-f8953c729333" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "112" :db/id 17592186280137}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186280137} :answer-field/id #uuid "13ebe4cc-aac8-5388-84d5-8872f110619f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186280865}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "566286c6-ab64-5382-ab24-0d1952795e00" :question/math-academy-id "q-163174" :question/problem "![](images/a6/a6910defd242e1b65b7bdf8b580cd2f56df3ac43951a9f83f353003e00a849b4.png)

A plate occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the lines $y=0$, $x=4$, and the curve $y=\sqrt{x}$, as shown above. If the mass density function of $D$ is given by $\lambda (x,y)=3y,$ find the moment of inertia of the lamina about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 4,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x}\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/dd/dd5ee021dd73317a775c0ea653212f7ee5545f8c6854e6a9daabdc93b5c3b9c0.png)

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 3y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}3{x}^{2}y+3{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{[\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{3}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{3}{2}{x}^{3}+\frac{3}{4}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3}{8}{x}^{4}+\frac{1}{4}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{4} \\  & =96+16 \\  & =112.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "9a3dcded-2a78-5806-a252-b52ade3817a0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481453}} {:db/id 17592186481469 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281637 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "839f5ece-276f-5816-96b9-c527a2493a8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2M}{3}" :db/id 17592186279770} {:answer/id #uuid "b9e6e3da-9c21-52c4-86e6-90e111164bf1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3M}{4}" :db/id 17592186280230} {:answer/id #uuid "d898035f-95c6-5b96-a44f-c85c5e0fb62a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{M}{3}" :db/id 17592186280506} {:answer/id #uuid "f28d76a8-28fa-5a01-aefa-cb1bdd261513" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2M" :db/id 17592186280703} {:answer/id #uuid "ffd690e9-c999-5620-b45c-5474e864788b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3M" :db/id 17592186280831}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279770} :answer-field/id #uuid "faab536c-ba69-524a-89bb-9d4a9ee45c2f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281279}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9a1f6eeb-74ef-55ae-8480-c174f3bc8d34" :question/math-academy-id "q-163219" :question/problem "![](images/c6/c683f411b11b7b353e166364c8e0fdbc0d218c07535c2f3430d832ab129702d8.png)

A triangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region $D$ enclosed between the $y$-axis and the lines $y=\frac{x}{2}$ and $y=3-x,$ as shown above. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,\frac{x}{2}\le y\le 3-x\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/6c/6c2cec5e919c25623396b5ba5f052481623a868c7520aa8e3d1d3eb34f3a4a58.png)

The area of the triangular plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 3=3.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x/2}^{3-x}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}[{\int }_{x/2}^{3-x}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}(3-x-\frac{x}{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}3{x}^{2}-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{[{x}^{3}-\frac{3}{8}{x}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{M}{3}(8-6) \\  & =\frac{2M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "de27f7da-aa86-5902-bdef-f289c3a397f0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481456}}] :activity/title "Moments of Inertia of Laminas About the Coordinate Axes" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186480735} {:db/id 17592186481447 :step/content {:db/id 17592186481404 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a9485ad-0d2d-50b4-b908-d8715c6808c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "75\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186480793} {:answer/id #uuid "1b253e13-148e-5e5e-a20a-b5b94224af45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "94.2\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186480795} {:answer/id #uuid "54795f54-0a40-564c-911b-ae120e159861" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "82\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186480891} {:answer/id #uuid "6d69e97d-0fc0-5bb2-b5a3-efd04876068d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "90\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186480945} {:answer/id #uuid "746e5210-a7d2-5781-83fe-86be72c56d8d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "86.4\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186480953}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186480945} :answer-field/id #uuid "362d2433-4c99-52b8-885b-22db14bc5af2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481257}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a91e5e5e-7869-5527-a5f1-b8a7012a6c8a" :question/math-academy-id "q-163171" :question/problem "A rectangular plate occupies the region

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\int }_{2}^{4}{x}^{2}\cdot x{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}[{\int }_{2}^{4}{x}^{3}{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{e}^{2y}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}]}_{2}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}60{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[30{e}^{2y}]_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =120-30 \\  & =90.\end{aligned}

Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type II region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,\frac{y}{3}\le x\le 4-y\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/47/47c897bd58a23965d9c36f683553c0817afa8bc2e37ed53a432edcd62b386e55.png)

The area of the triangular plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot 3=6.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{y/3}^{4-y}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}[{\int }_{y/3}^{4-y}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}(4-y-\frac{1}{3}y)\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{y}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{[\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{3}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{6}(36-27) \\  & =\frac{3M}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "63d1ac8f-1120-57bf-a3f2-068394de0e68" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481469}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3d50eaec-2761-511b-a299-ac2ff1333565" :answer/type {:db/id $$

$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,\frac{x}{2}\le y\le 3-x\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/6c/6c2cec5e919c25623396b5ba5f052481623a868c7520aa8e3d1d3eb34f3a4a58.png)

The area of the triangular plate $D$ is 

$$

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$

$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x/2}^{3-x}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}[{\int }_{x/2}^{3-x}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}(3-x-\frac{x}{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}3{x}^{2}-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{[{x}^{3}-\frac{3}{8}{x}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{M}{3}(8-6) \\  & =\frac{2M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "de27f7da-aa86-5902-bdef-f289c3a397f0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481456}} {:db/id 17592186481456 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281644 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24eeb6dc-6a62-5d90-a207-0acfc7258433" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186278919} {:answer/id #uuid "349f0582-d339-5e4d-9545-b31c93cda4da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{2}-1" :db/id 17592186279045} {:answer/id #uuid "538264a8-2746-5c22-950d-ad36b0c19129" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{2}-1}{8}" :db/id 17592186279351} {:answer/id #uuid "c7b8065a-0247-55f8-99df-fad5f0147068" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186280342} {:answer/id #uuid "f2ebd0da-d30a-58a4-863a-0db44212f7d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}" :db/id 17592186280710}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279351} :answer-field/id #uuid "ec2db863-9898-51d6-ba39-8b881e966e18" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281253}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b6b312d9-6efa-541f-ad5d-be93b575260c" :question/math-academy-id "q-163230" :question/problem "![](images/ad/ad7c939aded3f5e5e1e2f3b5e5743609e331625479c25f6a55659be730ed1cf5.png)

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le \sqrt[5]{2},\,\,\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=15r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}15r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}15{r}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}5{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & ={r}^{5}\,{|}_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}\cdot (-{cos}^{3}⁡\theta )\,{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3} \\  & =(2-1)\cdot (-\frac{1}{8}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}) \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}-1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6cb00066-5889-5430-a707-e706993fe08c"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24eeb6dc-6a62-5d90-a207-0acfc7258433" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 4,\,\,1\le y\le 3\},$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=3\cdot 2=6.$ 

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{x},$ we get

$$

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{x},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\cdot x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{2}^{4}x{y}^{4}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{4}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{2}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6{y}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{6}{5}{y}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}-0 \\  & =1.2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia of the lamina about the $x$-axis is $1.2\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$"} :step/id #uuid "c1f5cf58-a61e-50b5-be53-3c647dfe2618" :step/next {:db/id 17592186515679}} {:db/id 17592186515679 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281611 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00586df5-9953-5e7a-a58f-2329aa16a468" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186278586} {:answer/id #uuid "3bf84ed5-f917-50b8-8e4d-80368c472356" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279121} {:answer/id #uuid "4237198b-add2-521b-b160-d585a0924755" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279184} {:answer/id #uuid "58055d99-9594-5371-bd9f-20b8d761809d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279400} {:answer/id #uuid "86941ae5-17f0-581b-91b1-2673bcdf9949" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279793}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279121} :answer-field/id #uuid "945c0f7a-70d5-5057-8a4c-71bc5f6f818a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281099}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e73bf43d-4842-564c-b994-8b4ed88b9ee2" :question/math-academy-id "q-163146" :question/problem "A rectangular plate occupies the region

$$

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=1\cdot 3=3.$ 

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{3}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{7}{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{7M}{9}[y]_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{7M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
f(x) = 2x + 3
$$

and

$$
g(x) = x - 1
$$

The composite function can be calculated by taking the expression for the inner function ${\color{blue}g(x)}$ and passing it as input to the outer function $f({\color{blue}x})$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(f∘g)(x) &= f(g(x)) \\
&= 2(g(x)) + 3 \\
&= 2(x - 1) + 3 \\
&= 2x - 2 + 3 \\
&= 2x + 1
\end{aligned}
$$

So, we just take the expression for $f$ and replace every occurrence of $x$ with the expression for $g(x)$." :tutorial/id #uuid "7eaa8bd9-f7a4-5d70-b5f6-8cb47bd3a7bd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9264 "A polynomial of the form $a^3 + b^3$ is called a **sum of cubes**, while a polynomial of the form $a^3 – b^3$ is called a **difference of cubes**. 

Both of these polynomials follow a similar factor pattern:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{3}+{b}^{3} & =(a+b)({a}^{2}-ab+{b}^{2}) \\ {a}^{3}-{b}^{3} & =(a-b)({a}^{2}+ab+{b}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

One trick to memorizing the signs in these patterns is to use the mnemonic **SOAP**, which stands for **S**ame, **O**pposite, **A**lways **P**ositive.

- The sign of the linear factor is the **S**ame as that of the original polynomial,

- the first sign of the quadratic factor is the **O**pposite sign, and

- the last sign of the quadratic factor is **A**lways **P**ositive." :tutorial/id #uuid "6d37577f-b0f1-526c-a3cf-5c5c9b460f1e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3278 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id $$
a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2)
$$

we begin by expanding the right-hand side:

$$
(a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2) = a(a^2 - ab + b^2) + b(a^2 - ab + b^2)
$$

Now, we apply the distributive law to each term:

- For the first term, we have

$$
a(a^2 - ab + b^2) = a^3 - a^2b + ab^2.
$$

- For the second term, we have

$$
b(a^2 - ab + b^2) = a^2b - ab^2 + b^3.
$$

Adding both expressions gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(a+b)({a}^{2}-ab+{b}^{2}) & ={a}^{3}-{a}^{2}b+a{b}^{2}+{a}^{2}b-a{b}^{2}+{b}^{3} \\  & ={a}^{3}-\cancel{{a}^{2}b}+a{b}^{2}+\cancel{{a}^{2}b}-a{b}^{2}+{b}^{3} \\  & ={a}^{3}+a{b}^{2}-a{b}^{2}+{b}^{3} \\  & ={a}^{3}+\cancel{a{b}^{2}}-\cancel{a{b}^{2}}+{b}^{3} \\  & ={a}^{3}+{b}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

as required.

We can verify the formula for the difference in cubes, i.e. 

$$
a^3 - b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2)
$$

in a similar way." :tutorial/id #uuid "ac848e5f-adbe-580c-8672-c5d81e733624" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13258 :tutorial/title "Verifying the Sum of Cubes Formula"} :step/id #uuid "e28c781b-ff1b-5980-a480-c201af892698" :step/math-academy-id 461038}] :activity/title "Factoring Sums and Differences of Cubes" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186068970} {:db/id 17592186069643 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069967 :tutorial/content "A polynomial of the form $a^3 + b^3$ is called a **sum of cubes**, while a polynomial of the form $a^3 – b^3$ is called a **difference of cubes**.

:topic/math-academy-id 5289} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186205074 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205206 :tutorial/content "In previous lessons, we learned that the principal components of a standardized data matrix $X$ are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, and that these eigenvectors appear as the columns of $V$ in the singular value decomposition $X = U\Sigma V^T.$ We also learned that the variance along each principal component is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value.

In this lesson, we'll learn how to use principal components to perform **feature extraction** — the process of projecting high-dimensional data onto a lower-dimensional subspace while preserving as much variance as possible.

To illustrate the idea, suppose a biologist has recorded the resting heart rate and breathing rate for four mammals of different sizes. Both measurements have been standardized, giving the $4 \times 2$ data matrix

![](images/c6/c6952e27be521fed69a3e9ff76520b01873fdc3e3e28f0015550cbdc8cda3110.svg)

The biologist knows that body size strongly influences both heart rate and breathing rate — smaller animals tend to have faster rates for both. They want to extract a single "metabolic index" that captures this underlying factor. How should they proceed?

From the SVD $X = U\Sigma V^T,$ the first principal component is

![](images/82/82a177ec2b7448d62d171a249e464d5da15308e41a6140b156d2d50d2c251f00.svg)

which points in the direction of maximum variance. To obtain a one-dimensional representation of the data, we project each row of $X$ onto this direction by computing

![](images/39/39fa24e5c2dbec4ceb7a56c0ee17f9c4996d08a2d9e1bc91d0849d7e24abe5c1.svg)

The result is a $4 \times 1$ vector — one number per animal — that captures the variation in body size. The second animal, with the most negative standardized values (indicating a larger, slower-metabolizing animal), has the largest projected value." :tutorial/id #uuid "894cce51-8da3-55a0-8188-37b91ca5c47e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13253 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "95bf8e11-91d4-5faa-b4b9-f34fccb4a50e" :step/math-academy-id 629550 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205075}} {:db/id 17592186205075 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205213 :tutorial/content "More generally, suppose we have a standardized $n \times p$ data matrix $X,$ where each row is a data point and each column is a feature. To reduce the data from $p$ dimensions to $k$ dimensions, we project the data onto the first $k$ principal components. If $V_k$ is the $p \times k$ matrix whose columns are the first $k$ principal components, the reduced data matrix is

$$
Z = X V_k.
$$

Each row of $Z$ is a $k$-dimensional representation of the corresponding data point, expressed in terms of the principal component directions.

There is an equivalent way to compute $Z$ using the SVD. Starting from $X = U\Sigma V^T,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Z & =X{V}_{k} \\  & =UΣ{V}^{T}{V}_{k} \\  & =UΣ[\begin{aligned}{I}_{k} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =U[\begin{aligned}{Σ}_{k} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={U}_{k}{Σ}_{k},\end{aligned}
$$

where $U_k$ is the $n \times k$ matrix of the first $k$ columns of $U,$ and $\Sigma_k$ is the $k \times k$ diagonal matrix of the first $k$ singular values. 

So, we can compute the reduced data either as $XV_k$ or as $U_k\Sigma_k.$

**Watch out!** The vector $v_1$ (the first column of $V$) is a *direction* — a unit vector in feature space pointing along maximum variance. By contrast, the product $Xv_1$ (equivalently, $u_1\sigma_1$) is the *projected data* — an $n \times 1$ vector giving each data point's coordinate along that direction. Some texts refer to this projected data as "the first principal component of the data" or as "scores," so the term "principal component" can mean either the direction or the projected values, depending on context." :tutorial/id #uuid "41d5d02d-cb8d-54bf-9edc-b6d69f78b42e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14748 :tutorial/title "The Projection Formula"} :step/id #uuid "7cac9d17-5846-58de-95e6-7e0f8e56e0ac" :step/math-academy-id 629551 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205076}} {:db/id 17592186205076 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204105 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203875 :question/id #uuid "d6f2c4b7-eb2d-5d32-bcd8-8ec9443c14da" :question/math-academy-id "e-18786"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "de17e8f9-e3dc-5ba0-b6c9-327aa8cc10e0" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048654} {:db/id 17592186048721} {:db/id 17592186050539}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204594} {:db/id 17592186204611} {:db/id 17592186529096} {:db/id 17592186529104} {:db/id 17592186529111} {:db/id 17592186529129} {:db/id 17592186529136}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Best One Dimensional Reduction Given SVD of Data"} :step/id #uuid "74cf39f4-5e68-568e-bccb-a900bb795de7" :step/math-academy-id 629552 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205077}} {:db/id 17592186205077 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205214 :tutorial/content "In the previous section, we saw how to project data onto the first $k$ principal components. But how do we choose $k?$ Keeping more components preserves more information, while keeping fewer gives a more compact representation at the cost of discarding some variation.

Recall that the variance along the $i$th principal component is proportional to $\sigma_i^2,$ where $\sigma_i$ is the $i$th singular value. Therefore, the fraction of total variance preserved by keeping the first $k$ components is

$$
\dfrac{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \cdots + \sigma_k^2}{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \cdots + \sigma_p^2} = \dfrac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_i^2}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{p} \sigma_i^2}.
$$

While the amount of variance we need to preserve depends on the application, as a rule of thumb, we will choose the smallest $k$ that preserves at least $90\%$ of the variance. That is, we select $k$ such that

$$
\dfrac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_i^2}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{p} \sigma_i^2} \geq 0.90.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "97dbcb11-96a6-5a5f-aafc-7d212236c53c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14749 :tutorial/title "Choosing the Number of Components"} :step/id #uuid "0f3228b2-720c-5166-8dbe-667a26a03e21" :step/math-academy-id 629555 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205078}} {:db/id 17592186205078 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204106 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203876 :question/id #uuid "a17de4fa-f7c3-5038-b9fa-03780393b360" :question/math-academy-id "e-18840"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0bbf7902-3a15-5dd0-b2c8-e5b7fd541345" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204595} {:db/id 17592186204612} {:db/id 17592186529109} {:db/id 17592186529116} {:db/id 17592186529155} {:db/id 17592186529168}] :knowledge-point/title "Choosing the Amount of Dimensionality Reduction for a Given Dataset"} :step/id #uuid "e5823a48-e0f6-565c-9756-9e43c2763e07" :step/math-academy-id 629556 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205079}} {:db/id 17592186205079 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205215 :tutorial/content "We can now summarize the complete pipeline for using PCA to extract features from a dataset.

1\. **Standardize the data.** Subtract the mean of each feature and divide by its standard deviation. This ensures that all features contribute equally to the analysis, regardless of their original units or scales.

2\. **Compute the SVD.** Find the singular value decomposition $X_{\text{std}} = U\Sigma V^T.$ The columns of $V$ are the principal components, and the diagonal entries of $\Sigma$ are the singular values.

3\. **Choose the number of components.** Using the singular values, compute the cumulative variance for each possible choice of $k$ and select the smallest $k$ that preserves at least $90\%$ of the variance.

4\. **Project the data.** Compute the reduced data matrix $Z = X_{\text{std}} V_k,$ where $V_k$ consists of the first $k$ columns of $V.$

To interpret results in terms of the original features or to apply the same transformation to new data, we must keep track of the means and standard deviations used in Step 1." :tutorial/id #uuid "3cf2cdec-09e3-5344-84d2-4617e6830871" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14750 :tutorial/title "The Feature Extraction Pipeline"} :step/id #uuid "cc9242f2-052f-51db-9396-bda401bd5870" :step/math-academy-id 629559 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205080}} {:db/id 17592186205080 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204107 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203877 :question/id #uuid "dcbf83b0-b552-52d6-97d3-9bc3ac6b0823" :question/math-academy-id "e-18844"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "45f11c96-89e5-5662-81b6-06cff80a4cf2" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204604} {:db/id 17592186204613} {:db/id 17592186529174}] :knowledge-point/title "Using PCA to Dimensionally Reduce an Uncentered Dataset"} :step/id #uuid "f79c44a0-cf86-5bde-a18b-20df7fdcba79" :step/math-academy-id 629560}] :activity/title "Feature Extraction Using PCA" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186204154} {:db/id 17592186205074 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205206 :tutorial/content "In previous lessons, we learned that the principal components of a standardized data matrix $X$ are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, and that these eigenvectors appear as the columns of $V$ in the singular value decomposition $X = U\Sigma V^T.$ We also learned that the variance along each principal component is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value.

$$

where $U_k$ is the $n \times k$ matrix of the first $k$ columns of $U,$ and $\Sigma_k$ is the $k \times k$ diagonal matrix of the first $k$ singular values. 

So, we can compute the reduced data either as $XV_k$ or as $U_k\Sigma_k.$

**Watch out!** The vector $v_1$ (the first column of $V$) is a *direction* — a unit vector in feature space pointing along maximum variance. By contrast, the product $Xv_1$ (equivalently, $u_1\sigma_1$) is the *projected data* — an $n \times 1$ vector giving each data point's coordinate along that direction. Some texts refer to this projected data as "the first principal component of the data" or as "scores," so the term "principal component" can mean either the direction or the projected values, depending on context." :tutorial/id #uuid "41d5d02d-cb8d-54bf-9edc-b6d69f78b42e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14748 :tutorial/title "The Projection Formula"} :step/id #uuid "7cac9d17-5846-58de-95e6-7e0f8e56e0ac" :step/math-academy-id 629551 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205076}} {:db/id 17592186205213 :tutorial/content "More generally, suppose we have a standardized $n \times p$ data matrix $X,$ where each row is a data point and each column is a feature. $$

But how do we choose $k?$ Keeping more components preserves more information, while keeping fewer gives a more compact representation at the cost of discarding some variation.

Recall that the variance along the $i$th principal component is proportional to $\sigma_i^2,$ where $\sigma_i$ is the $i$th singular value. Therefore, the fraction of total variance preserved by keeping the first $k$ components is

$$
\dfrac{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \cdots + \sigma_k^2}{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \cdots + \sigma_p^2} = \dfrac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_i^2}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{p} \sigma_i^2}.
$$

While the amount of variance we need to preserve depends on the application, as a rule of thumb, we will choose the smallest $k$ that preserves at least $90\%$ of the variance. That is, we select $k$ such that

$$
\dfrac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_i^2}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{p} \sigma_i^2} \geq 0.90.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "97dbcb11-96a6-5a5f-aafc-7d212236c53c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14749 :tutorial/title "Choosing the Number of Components"} :step/id #uuid "0f3228b2-720c-5166-8dbe-667a26a03e21" :step/math-academy-id 629555 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205078}} {:db/id 17592186205214 :tutorial/content "In the previous section, we saw how to project data onto the first $k$ principal components. 1\. **Standardize the data.** Subtract the mean of each feature and divide by its standard deviation. This ensures that all features contribute equally to the analysis, regardless of their original units or scales.

2\. **Compute the SVD.** Find the singular value decomposition $X_{\text{std}} = U\Sigma V^T.$ The columns of $V$ are the principal components, and the diagonal entries of $\Sigma$ are the singular values.

3\. **Choose the number of components.** Using the singular values, compute the cumulative variance for each possible choice of $k$ and select the smallest $k$ that preserves at least $90\%$ of the variance.

4\. **Project the data.** Compute the reduced data matrix $Z = X_{\text{std}} V_k,$ where $V_k$ consists of the first $k$ columns of $V.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(y+5)^{2}}{5}-(x-2)^{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(y+5)^{2}}{5}-(0-2)^{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(y+5)^{2}}{5}-4 & =1 \\ \frac{(y+5)^{2}}{5} & =5 \\ (y+5)^{2} & =25 \\ y+5 & =\pm 5 \\ y & =-10,0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =12 \\ (-4)^{2}-{y}^{2} & =12 \\ 16-{y}^{2} & =12 \\ -{y}^{2} & =12-16 \\ -{y}^{2} & =-4 \\ {y}^{2} & =4 \\ y & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that this hyperbola intersects the $x$-axis at two points. How do we find the coordinates of these points?

![](images/a3/a3f664f7e1916ca550c33060d78ad26e33aa9eb78ba32a44d46d7aa109ed4c2a.png)

To find the coordinates of the $x$-intercepts of a hyperbola, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the hyperbola and solve the resulting equation for $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =9 \\ x & =\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $x$-intercepts are $(-3,0)$ and $(3,0).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "af9cbb7e-1a39-5ea6-9000-606a1e7bfa33" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4585 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid $$

&= 3 \cdot 0.2 \\
&= 0.6
\end{aligned}

[{:db/id 17592186111495 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111880 :tutorial/content "The **power rule** allows us to simplify logarithms of exponentiated expressions. It states that

$$
\log_{n}\left(c^{\color{blue}m} \right) = {\color{blue}m}\log_{n}{c}
$$

In other words, the logarithm has the effect of "bringing down the power."

For example, let's use the rule to simplify

$$
\log\left(125\right)
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log (125) &= \log (5^{3}) \\
&= 3\log (5)
\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** To understand why the power rule works, notice that we can reach the same result using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log (125) &= \log (5^{3}) \\
&= \log (5 \cdot 5 \cdot 5) \\
&= \log (5) + \log (5) + \log (5) \\
&= 3\log (5)
\end{aligned}
$$

The power rule is just a shortcut for the above procedure." :tutorial/id #uuid "3cb8c8f4-3573-58ab-8e08-3c60cc3a3d12" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2795 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid 360^\circ$. If the solutions $\theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3, \theta_4$ are written in ascending order, then what is the numerical value of $\theta_2\cdot \theta_3$?" :question/worked-solution "Note that the function $\tan{\theta}$ is not defined at

$$
\theta = 90^\circ, 270^\circ
$$

so these values cannot be solutions to the equation.

First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{3}\sin θ\tan θ - \sin θ &= 0 \\
\sin θ(\sqrt{3}\tan θ - 1) &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

By the zero-product property, we have to solve two equations:

$$
\sin{\theta} = 0, \qquad \sqrt{3}\tan{\theta} - 1 =0
$$

Let's solve each equation separately.

- First, we solve $\sin{\theta} = 0$. The solutions to this equation for $0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ$ are $\theta = 0^\circ, \, 180^\circ$.
- Then, we solve $\sqrt{3}\tan{\theta} - 1 =0$, or equivalently $\tan{\theta} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$. The solutions to this equation for $0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ$ are $\theta=30^\circ, \, 210^\circ$.

Combining all solutions from both equations, we get

$$
\theta_1 = 0^\circ, \quad \theta_2= 30^\circ, \quad \theta_3=180^\circ, \quad \theta_4= 210^\circ
$$

Finally,

$$
\theta_2\cdot \theta_3 =30 \cdot 180 = 5\,400
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048402} {:db/id 17592186049568} {:db/id 17592186050105} {:db/id 17592186050497} {:db/id 17592186111008 :question/id #uuid "06299d69-011f-54ac-acef-b8d0dbf13780" :question/math-academy-id "q-23994"} {:db/id 17592186111009 :question/id #uuid "2b6ca370-aeff-55c8-b89d-1d1d2364acd0" :question/math-academy-id "q-24000"} {:db/id 17592186110683 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110461 :question/id #uuid "ef4a57fd-8ade-5b7d-9d6e-0fabd228e603" :question/math-academy-id "e-3546"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b8553da6-42ce-5b77-97c4-7d9e2ee55f85" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186111007 :question/id #uuid "a9169812-d08e-55f1-8cd5-256a76a7c044" :question/math-academy-id "q-23992"} {:db/id 17592186111010 :question/id #uuid "e42167e1-42b5-5316-b2f2-add419b65958" :question/math-academy-id "q-24002"}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Trigonometric Equation by Rearranging the Equation and Then Factoring"} {:db/id 17592186110461 :question/id #uuid "ef4a57fd-8ade-5b7d-9d6e-0fabd228e603" :question/math-academy-id "e-3546" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186110683 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b8553da6-42ce-5b77-97c4-7d9e2ee55f85" :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Trigonometric Equation by Rearranging the Equation and Then Factoring"}] :question/problem "Consider the equation $\sqrt{2} \sin{x} \cos{x} = -\sin{x}$ for $0 \leq x \leq \pi$. If the solutions $x_1, x_2, x_3$ are written in ascending order, then what is $x_2\cdot x_3$?" :question/worked-solution "First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{2}\sin x\cos x &= -\sin x \\
\sqrt{2}\sin x\cos x + \sin x &= 0 \\
\sin x(\sqrt{2}\cos x + 1) &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

By the zero-product property, we have to solve two equations:

$$
\sin{x} = 0, \qquad \sqrt{2} \cos{x} + 1 =0
$$

Let's solve each equation separately.

- First, we solve $\sin{x} = 0$. The solutions to this equation for $0\leq x \leq \pi$ are $x = 0,\, \pi$.
- Then, we solve $\sqrt{2} \cos{x} + 1= 0$, or equivalently $\cos{x} =-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$. The solution to this equation for $0\leq x \leq \pi$ is $x =\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

Combining all solutions from both equations, we get

$$
x_1 = 0,\quad x_2=\dfrac{3\pi}{4},\quad x_3= \pi
$$

Finally,

$$
x_2\cdot x_3 = \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \cdot \pi=\dfrac{3\pi^2}{4}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186111007 :question/id #uuid "a9169812-d08e-55f1-8cd5-256a76a7c044" :question/math-academy-id "q-23992"} {:db/id 17592186111010 :question/id #uuid "e42167e1-42b5-5316-b2f2-add419b65958" :question/math-academy-id "q-24002" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186110683 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b8553da6-42ce-5b77-97c4-7d9e2ee55f85" :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Trigonometric Equation by Rearranging the Equation and Then Factoring"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8e58287a-4ed3-5565-8b30-1d607c85dbaa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{4π^{2}}{9}" :db/id 17592186107764} {:answer/id #uuid "a752ec47-dda1-5ea2-82d3-2c8db9f522ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{π^{2}}{3}" :db/id 17592186107765} {:answer/id #uuid "b481fd2d-1f2c-509a-a639-394f0543f57e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2π^{2}}{3}" :db/id 17592186107766} {:answer/id #uuid "be5839e3-e77c-5453-893e-bba6d562a31f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{π^{2}}{9}" :db/id 17592186107767} {:answer/id #uuid "6afda1d5-bf04-5849-acce-30e908b96c7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186107768}] :answer-field/id #uuid "039d55a3-f5ec-5e3a-b6e9-2733fee9f9fb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186107763}] :question/problem "Consider the equation $2\sin x\cos x =-\sin x$ for $- π \le x < π$. $$
\sin{x} = 0
$$

On the interval

$$
0^\circ \leq x < 360^\circ
$$

the excluded values are

$$
x = 0^\circ, 180^\circ
$$

On the other hand, the function $\tan{x}$ is not defined at the points where

$$
\cos{x} = 0
$$

In the given interval, the excluded values are

$$
x = 90^\circ, 270^\circ
$$

First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\csc x\tan x &= \tan x \\
\csc x\tan x - \tan x &= 0 \\
(\csc x - 1)\tan x &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the zero-product property, we have to solve two equations:

$$
\csc{x} - 1 = 0, \qquad \tan{x} = 0
$$

Let's solve each equation separately.

- First, we solve $\csc{x} -1= 0$, or equivalently, $\csc x=1$. The solution to this equation for $0 ^\circ \leq x \lt 360^\circ$ is $x = 90^\circ$.
- Then, we solve $\tan{x} = 0$. The solutions to this equation for $0^\circ\leq x \lt 360^\circ$ are $x = 0^\circ,\, 180^\circ$.

Finally, taking into account the values excluded from the interval, we conclude that the given equation has no solution."} {:db/id 17592186048533} {:db/id 17592186049220} {:db/id 17592186050313} {:db/id 17592186111146 :question/id #uuid "4dc987a8-ede8-5bf8-ab3e-da512cbfba1e" :question/math-academy-id "q-30182"} {:db/id 17592186111147 :question/id #uuid "59756d3c-3c85-5289-a62f-143fdaa1a9c9" :question/math-academy-id "q-30184" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186110684 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8f0f24e0-da03-5fa3-b3dc-bb383068ae15" :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Trigonometric Equation Containing Reciprocal Functions by Factoring"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "81a2d678-ca5a-5292-b468-14a52e3572f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "7200" :db/id 17592186108618} {:answer/id #uuid "e447c647-cc52-5cc5-ba96-a27ba50f45d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4500" :db/id 17592186108619} {:answer/id #uuid "f2342dd8-6ede-5787-b191-4571cfbcb0e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "18000" :db/id 17592186108620} {:answer/id #uuid "125b0884-2248-5f55-a7e9-068076603ec8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2250" :db/id 17592186108621} {:answer/id #uuid "57309f16-2aa5-51d5-8971-b6d997ad293d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "9000" :db/id 17592186108622}] :answer-field/id #uuid "5b13f2ce-c29b-57af-9ebe-adda59545e9e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186108617}] :question/problem "Given that $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $2\sin x\sec x - \sec x = 0$ for $0^{∘} \le x < 360^{∘}$, what is the numerical value of $x_{1} \cdot x_{2}$?

The curves intersect at the points $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$, as shown. Find $x$-coordinates of these points.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
2\cos x\sin x - \cos x &= 0 \\
\cos x(2\sin x - 1) &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\cos{x} = 0, \qquad 2\sin{x} - 1 = 0
$$

Let's solve each equation separately.

- First, we solve $\cos{x} = 0$. The solutions to this equation for $0^\circ \leq x < 360^\circ$ are $x= 90^\circ, \, 270^\circ$.
- Then, we solve $2\sin{x} - 1 = 0$, or equivalently $\sin{x}=\dfrac{1}{2}$. The solutions to this equation for $0^\circ \leq x < 360^\circ$ are $x = 30^\circ,\, 150^\circ$.

Combining all solutions from both equations, we get

$$
x_1=30^\circ, \quad x_2=90^\circ,\quad x_3=150^\circ, \quad x_4 = 270^\circ
$$"} {:db/id 17592186111148 :question/id #uuid "11dba21b-1d17-5273-96c1-1c2aff4558fc" :question/math-academy-id "q-30188"} {:db/id 17592186111180 :question/id #uuid [{:db/id 17592186111625 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111868 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find all of the solutions to the equation

$$
\sin{x}\cos{x}-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin{x} = 0, \qquad 0^\circ \leq x \leq 180^\circ
$$

First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin x\cos x - \frac{1}{2}\sin x &= 0 \\
\sin x(\cos x - \frac{1}{2}) &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

We can now apply the zero product rule, which states that $ab=0$ if and only if $a=0$ or $b=0$. This gives us two equations,

$$
\sin{x} = 0 \quad \textrm{and} \quad \cos{x}-\dfrac12=0
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- First, we solve $\sin{x}=0$. The solutions to this equation that lie in the given domain are $x = 0^\circ$ and $x=180^\circ$.
- Then, we solve $\cos{x}-\dfrac12=0$, or equivalently, $\cos{x}=\dfrac12$. The only solution to this equation that lies in the given domain is $x = 60^\circ$.

Combining all the solutions from both equations, the solutions of the original equation (in ascending order) are

$$
x_1 = 0^\circ,\quad x_2 = 60^\circ,\quad x_3 = 180^\circ

For example, suppose we want to find all of the solutions to the equation

$$
(\sec x -1)(2\sin x +1)= 0, \qquad -\pi \leq x < \pi
$$

First, note that the function $\sec{x}$ is not defined at the points where $\cos{x}=0$. On the interval $[-\pi,\pi)$, the excluded values are

$$
x=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}
$$

The equation is already factored, so by the zero-product property, we have to solve two equations:

$$
\sec{x} -1 =0, \qquad 2\sin{x} + 1 = 0
$$

Let's solve each equation separately.

- First, we solve $\sec{x} -1 =0$, or equivalently, $\sec{x} =1$. The only solution to this equation for $-\pi \leq x < \pi$ is $x = 0$.
- Then, we solve $2\sin{x} + 1 = 0$, or equivalently, $\sin{x} = -\dfrac12$. The solutions to this equation for $-\pi \leq x < \pi$ are $x=-\dfrac{5\pi}{6},-\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

Combining all the solutions from both equations, the solutions to the original equation (in ascending order) are

$$
x_1 =-\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\quad x_2 =-\dfrac{\pi}{6},\quad x_3 = 0
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e82f262f-fd25-5e1a-90d3-7bdfe8e09095" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2576 :tutorial/title "Equations Containing Reciprocal Functions"} :step/id #uuid "ad98517c-7c49-5633-9f3e-c8a05d2183ff" :step/math-academy-id 447711 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111629}} {:db/id 17592186111629 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110684 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110463 :question/id #uuid "362274e9-6980-5e3b-896b-db42cfc41a9e" :question/math-academy-id "e-3550"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8f0f24e0-da03-5fa3-b3dc-bb383068ae15" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048533} {:db/id 17592186049220} {:db/id 17592186050313}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186111146} {:db/id 17592186111147}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Trigonometric Equation Containing Reciprocal Functions by Factoring"} :step/id #uuid "1f25f832-b48a-569a-9d0c-eaa3b450bf16" :step/math-academy-id 447712 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111630}} {:db/id 17592186111630 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110685 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110464 :question/id #uuid "0aff48c8-380d-504b-a044-8ba08a2617a4" :question/math-academy-id "e-3551"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9dea3f3b-5c9b-5005-996a-792a6902fcce" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186111148} {:db/id 17592186111180}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Some Coordinates on a Graph by Solving a Trigonometric Equation"} :step/id #uuid "00f0cdfe-17ea-519e-94fc-30cb570c2406" :step/math-academy-id 447715}] :activity/title "Solving Trigonometric Equations Using the Zero-Product Property" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186110840} {:db/id 17592186111625 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111868 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find all of the solutions to the equation

$$
\sin{x}\cos{x}-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin{x} = 0, \qquad 0^\circ \leq x \leq 180^\circ
$$

First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin x\cos x - \frac{1}{2}\sin x &= 0 \\
\sin x(\cos x - \frac{1}{2}) &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

We can now apply the zero product rule, which states that $ab=0$ if and only if $a=0$ or $b=0$. This gives us two equations,

$$
\sin{x} = 0 \quad \textrm{and} \quad \cos{x}-\dfrac12=0
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- First, we solve $\sin{x}=0$. The solutions to this equation that lie in the given domain are $x = 0^\circ$ and $x=180^\circ$.
- Then, we solve $\cos{x}-\dfrac12=0$, or equivalently, $\cos{x}=\dfrac12$. The only solution to this equation that lies in the given domain is $x = 60^\circ$.

Combining all the solutions from both equations, the solutions of the original equation (in ascending order) are

$$
x_1 = 0^\circ,\quad x_2 = 60^\circ,\quad x_3 = 180^\circ
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f48575a8-2964-5b25-9b20-92588072e29d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2575 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "da9cf3f1-fc61-57da-8b19-93d0f6af8437" :step/math-academy-id 447704 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111626}} {:db/id 17592186111868 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find all of the solutions to the equation

{:db/id 17592186193899 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed *continuous* random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta),$ then the likelihood function $L(\theta)$ of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is given by

$$
L(\theta) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta)
$$

where $f(x;\theta)$ is the probability density function of $X_i$ for $i=1,2,\ldots, n,$ and $\theta$ is an unknown parameter.

Similar to the case of discrete random variables, the **log-likelihood function** is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(L(\theta )) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta )) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{1};\,\theta )\cdot f({x}_{2};\,\theta )⋯f({x}_{n};\,\theta )) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{1};\,\theta ))+\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{2};\,\theta ))+⋯+\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{n};\,\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\,\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{3}\le \theta \le \pi ,$ shown above?" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{5-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186172289 :question/id #uuid "f58568c3-ce47-5162-ad81-da8c754e43d8" :question/math-academy-id "q-123439" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid $$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={sec}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({sec}^{3}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(3{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sec}^{6}⁡\theta +9{sec}^{6}⁡\theta {tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sec}^{6}⁡\theta (1+9{tan}^{2}⁡\theta })\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \sqrt{1+9{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=4+\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta .

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{(4+\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta )^{2}+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{16+8\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡4\theta +16{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{16+8\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta +1+15{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{17+8\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta +15{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}

the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Where $1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta>0$, $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}.
$$

Applying the arc-length formula piecewise between the finitely many zeros of $r$, the expression for our line integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{(\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta })^{2}+{(\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )+\frac{4{cos}^{2}⁡4\theta }{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )^{2}+4(1-{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta )}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )^{2}+4(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )[1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta +4-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta ]}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{5-3\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}

"![](images/3b/3b8ef36c29d1babc5c3ccf1d474678a18ed5937b883e026d18d5c7ea1aaaa3f5.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=3+\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ,$ shown above?" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=3+\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(3+\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta )^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9+6\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡3\theta +9{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9+6\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta +1+8{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{10+6\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta +8{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186447160 :question/id #uuid "fb00dc0e-66fe-5382-b23d-00ac1fa661b6" :question/math-academy-id "q-123559"} {:db/id 17592186483352 :question/id #uuid "22b679e5-bd2f-5f85-b6e8-97dc0feb70a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-149799" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d1c4079-2e4b-58ce-bcdd-cef5dccc4c25" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{\theta }\sqrt{2{\theta }^{2}+2\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186482832} {:answer/id #uuid "2dfd78b7-9d7a-58b9-8cb4-d7bec505415d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{\theta {e}^{\theta }+1}\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186482890} {:answer/id #uuid "33feb924-d253-5720-9471-b530f5057780" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{\theta }\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}+1}\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186482903} {:answer/id #uuid "4170ee29-2690-59a0-ac02-7ef811bc4abc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}{e}^{2\theta }+1}\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186482922} {:answer/id #uuid "42a9d64f-13f1-500c-89f4-8b8e1616488f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{2\theta }\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}+2}\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186482925}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186482832} :answer-field/id #uuid "a8b124e2-32da-5651-8541-39b8419c32ee" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186483305}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\theta {e}^{\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi \,?$" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},$ shown above." :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{4+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{8}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{8}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =8(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186483419 :question/id #uuid "dcd1fd46-503a-5471-9362-496d88e411cc" :question/math-academy-id "q-149819" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "614ec109-ddf5-5d69-8b6f-788cffd7d795" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186482983} {:answer/id #uuid "654af1d0-1b91-562a-9226-854b3fe81f62" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186482990} {:answer/id #uuid "6bec234f-7e3b-515c-a2ad-33a2c8025357" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\pi " :db/id 17592186482999} {:answer/id #uuid "960e21ae-a0b1-56a4-a8e3-7aa555730f7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186483072} {:answer/id #uuid "c60010fa-7943-5d78-8597-6d6fec062ebb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi " :db/id 17592186483143}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186482983} :answer-field/id #uuid "87114391-cb4d-5092-83cc-b2e18baed326" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186483291}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "![](images/c7/c700a13da4a3b21940ec6268a89670eee850fc6206285bd3b444959a8b386276.png)

\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={cos}^{3}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}){cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}).

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\sqrt{{({cos}^{3}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}))}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}){cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}))}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\sqrt{{cos}^{6}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})+{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}){cos}^{4}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\sqrt{{cos}^{4}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})[{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})+{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})]}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\sqrt{{cos}^{4}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}[1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\theta }{3})]\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[\theta +\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\theta }{3})]}_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}

Since $r=\sqrt{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\,$ we have

\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}.

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{(\sqrt{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta })^{2}+{(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )+\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡2\theta }{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )^{2}+{cos}^{2}⁡2\theta }{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡2\theta }{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{2-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,\theta {|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =\sqrt{2}\text{ }(\pi -\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
