:step/math-academy-id 35543 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172997}} {:db/id 17592186172995 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173201 :tutorial/content "Recall that for a path $C$ in the $xy$-plane, the arc length $L$ of $C$ can be computed as the line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C\mathbin{:}$

$$
L = \displaystyle\int_C \, \textrm{d}s
$$

Now, if $C$ is defined parametrically as 

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t),\, y(t)\rangle, \quad a\leq t \leq b ,
$$

then we can also calculate the arc length of $C$ as

$$
L = \int_{a}^{b}||\mathbf r'(t)||\,\textrm d t = \int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t\,.
$$

By comparing our two expressions for $L,$ we say that the **arc-length element** $\textrm ds$ for a parametrically defined curve is given by

$$
\textrm ds = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t\,.
$$

Geometrically, we can think of $\textrm ds$ as representing the change in arc length that arises due to a vanishingly small change in $t.$ By summing (integrating) all of these small changes, we arrive at the arc length of $C.$ We'll explore this in more detail at the end of the lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "56e8bdd3-5303-5eeb-82d3-ef837773c38f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5797 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "65361afd-5d8b-59a0-8bed-041764bc0685" :step/math-academy-id 35544 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172996}} {:db/id 17592186172996 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173202 :tutorial/content "Now suppose that a curve $C$ is defined using plane polar coordinates as

$$
r = r(\theta), \qquad \theta_1\leq\theta\leq\theta_2.
$$

We've already seen that a polar curve is just a special type of parametric curve in the parameter $\theta,$ where

$$
x = r(\theta)\cos\theta, \qquad y = r(\theta)\sin\theta, \qquad \theta_1\leq\theta\leq\theta_2.
$$

Using the usual formula for the arc length of a polar curve, the arc length of $C$ can be calculated as

$$
L = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta
$$

which is the same as the line integral

$$
L = \displaystyle\int\limits_C \, \textrm{d}s.
$$

By comparing our two expressions for $L,$ the arc-length element $\textrm ds$ for a curve can also be defined using polar coordinates as follows:

$$
\textrm ds = \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta
$$

We'll build up a geometric understanding of this result at the end of the lesson. $$

$$
\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & ≈||Δr|{|}^{2} \\  & ={(Δx)}^{2}+{(Δy)}^{2} \\  & ≈{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}Δt)}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}Δt)}^{2} \\  & ={(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}(Δt)^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}(Δt)^{2} \\  & =[{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}](Δt)^{2}.\end{aligned}

$$
\textrm d s

=

$$

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b310dc84-9da7-5492-9639-145086fe7403" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5803 :tutorial/title "Geometric Interpretation of the Arc Length Element for a Polar Curve"} :step/id #uuid "6cd1a226-a48b-5c1c-9eed-9c80bd2de431" :step/math-academy-id 35570}] :activity/title "Further Properties of Line Integrals of Scalar Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186172176} {:db/id 17592186172995 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173201 :tutorial/content "Recall that for a path $C$ in the $xy$-plane, the arc length $L$ of $C$ can be computed as the line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C\mathbin{:}$

$$
L = \displaystyle\int_C \, \textrm{d}s
$$

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t),\, y(t)\rangle, \quad a\leq t \leq b ,

then we can also calculate the arc length of $C$ as

$$

$$

arrive at the arc length of $C.$ We'll explore this in more detail at the end of the lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "56e8bdd3-5303-5eeb-82d3-ef837773c38f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5797 :tutorial/title Now, the change in arc length $\Delta s$ can be approximated as the magnitude of $\Delta \mathbf r.$ Since our two components are perpendicular, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & ≈||Δr|{|}^{2} \\  & ≈(Δr)^{2}+(rΔ\theta )^{2} \\  & =Δ{r}^{2}+{r}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that a difference quotient can be approximated as derivative, we have

$$
\Delta r = r(\theta + \Delta\theta) - r(\theta) = \dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\Delta\theta.
$$

Substituting this into our expression for $(\Delta s)^2$ above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & ≈{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2}+{r}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2} \\  & ={r}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2} \\  & =[{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}](Δ\theta )^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Delta s = \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\Delta\theta.
$$

If we imagine the limiting case where $\Delta \theta \to 0,$ we arrive at the arc length element $\textrm d s\mathbin{:}$

$$
\textrm d s

=

\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\textrm d\theta

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$

Since $r={cos}^{3}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}){cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}).

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\sqrt{{({cos}^{3}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}))}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}){cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}))}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\sqrt{{cos}^{6}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})+{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}){cos}^{4}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\sqrt{{cos}^{4}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})[{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})+{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})]}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\sqrt{{cos}^{4}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}[1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\theta }{3})]\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[\theta +\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\theta }{3})]}_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ,$ shown above?" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ,$ shown above?" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1+{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1+1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "f880bd39-bc57-5d41-b262-cb0554da3861" :step/next {:db/id 17592186483454}} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046644} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186511645} :activity/id #uuid Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},$ shown above." :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}-\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})}) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\cdot (\sqrt{2}-0) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "f7f86389-8351-5a11-bac8-76649d974f77"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "06dd37ec-93a9-5b21-89e4-561d7cf50bec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int $$

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(e^x) = e^x,
$$

we begin with the definition of the derivative:

where $f(x) = e^x$.

Substituting the function $f(x)$ into the definition of $f'(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x+h}-{e}^{x}}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{h}-{e}^{x}}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}\cdot ({e}^{h}-1)}{h} \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{h}-1}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, it can be shown that

$$
\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{e^h - 1}{h} = 1,
$$

which gives

$$
f'(x) = e^x \cdot 1 = e^x.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(e^x) = e^x.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1b006e01-04f6-5f6b-b435-b0f89163d7a1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2613 :tutorial/title "Justifying the Rule for the Derivative of the Exponential Function"} :step/id #uuid "be9c264f-1e13-55c5-83f7-3217ce14b437" :step/math-academy-id 12311 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097749}} {:db/id 17592186097749 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097806 :tutorial/content "Now, let's derive the rule

$$

Now, it can be shown that

$$
\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{e^h - 1}{h} = 1,
$$

which gives

$$

$$

$$

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Given the singular value decomposition $A=UΣ{V}^{T},$ where $A$ is a $5\times 3$ matrix, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $Σ$ is a $5\times 3$ matrix
- **II.** $Σ$ is a diagonal matrix with only positive elements on the main diagonal
- **III.** $V$ is a $3\times 3$ orthogonal matrix" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of an $m\times n$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $m\times n$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $m\times m$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $n\times n$ matrix.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $5\times 3$ matrix, $Σ$ must be a $5\times 3$ matrix.

- Statement II is false. The matrix $Σ$ in the singular value decomposition $UΣ{V}^{T}$ must be diagonal with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal. The main diagonal may contain zeroes.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $5\times 3$ matrix, $V$ in the singular value decomposition $UΣ{V}^{T}$ must be a $3\times 3$ orthogonal matrix.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186399295 :question/id #uuid "eab879a0-3375-58dd-903d-5ef4248752b2" :question/math-academy-id "q-96231"} {:db/id 17592186418155 From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that the singular values are ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$ So, the first column of $V$ corresponds to the singular value ${\sigma }_{1}=9.$

Hence, we need to find a unit eigenvector of ${A}^{T}\,A$ that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=81.$ Computing ${A}^{T}\,A-81I,$ we get

$$

$$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T \! A$):

- For $\lambda_1=\sigma_1^2=81,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-81I & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & -24 \\ -24 & 73\end{bmatrix}-81\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-72 & -24 \\ -24 & -8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}17 & 8 \\ 8 & 17\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=3.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=25,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}17 & 8 \\ 8 & 17\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-8 & 8 \\ 8 & -8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-25I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=9,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-9I & =\begin{bmatrix}17 & 8 \\ 8 & 17\end{bmatrix}-9\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8 & 8 \\ 8 & 8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-9I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186383445 :question/id #uuid "dbd7a90d-1fca-5332-9851-2184d13895b4" :question/math-academy-id "q-140645"} {:db/id 17592186395086 :question/id #uuid "5db18361-738b-5a9a-b3b0-1db51bcde1bd" :question/math-academy-id "q-95911" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186162019 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e9466d5b-d361-5504-8e16-99f87210e808" :knowledge-point/title "The Singular Value Decomposition of a 2x2 Matrix"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "332ee583-e727-5bba-8acd-922d23695b56" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}$

$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=10$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=5.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=100,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-100I & =\begin{bmatrix}85 & 30 \\ 30 & 40\end{bmatrix}-100\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-15 & 30 \\ 30 & -60\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-100I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=25,$ we have

$$

A=\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}8 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & 1 \\ -4 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}37 & -18 \\ -18 & 52\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=8$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=5.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=64,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-64I & =\begin{bmatrix}37 & -18 \\ -18 & 52\end{bmatrix}-64\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-27 & -18 \\ -18 & -12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-64I)x=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=25,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}37 & -18 \\ -18 & 52\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}12 & -18 \\ -18 & 27\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-25I)x=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{24}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{16}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{10}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{15}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186520509 :question/id #uuid "eeba80ad-bee9-5269-baef-fbd3bd2d6cda" :question/math-academy-id "q-96323" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2b2efb8c-2656-5a9e-bdf4-74177ad5bfa0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=81,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-81I & =[\begin{aligned}73 & -24 \\ -24 & 9\end{aligned}]-81[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-8 & -24 \\ -24 & -72\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-81I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-I & =[\begin{aligned}73 & -24 \\ -24 & 9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}72 & -24 \\ -24 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
A=U \Sigma V^T,
$$

where

- $\Sigma$ is an $m \times n$ matrix with the singular values of $A$ (ordered from largest to smallest) on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $m \times m$ matrix, and

- $V$ is an orthogonal $n \times n$ matrix.

The columns of $U$ are called the **left singular vectors** of $A,$ and the columns of $V$ are called the **right singular vectors** of $A.$

For example, the matrix ![](images/46/46b29ceb84e2ed98e48642e67277c9bf63d0552bcd07f813a9ffcaf665ff91b7.svg) has the following singular value decomposition:

![](images/29/298933eb0a789ebe57a296088172f6927d1573770824c0b0cffb393eb9894c70.svg)

The singular value decomposition of a matrix $A$ can be thought of as a type of diagonalization that works for *any* $m\times n$ matrix! It's also one of linear algebra's most useful forms of matrix factorization with applications in statistics, image compression, machine learning, and more." :tutorial/id #uuid ![](images/61/61ff6d3a83c2a660ca8369d96ab7bede86f9a124727db8d5a7e320dcd5aaad74.svg)

Suppose we're given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A.$ Let's use this information to find the matrix $U.$

From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that the singular values are $\color{blue}\sigma_1=9$ and $\color{red}\sigma_2=1.$ 

Earlier, we saw that the columns of $\mathbf u$ are given by

$$
\mathbf{u}_i = \dfrac{1}{\sigma_i} A\mathbf{v}_i
$$

where $\mathbf u_i$ and $\mathbf v_i$ are the $i$th columns of the matrices $U$ and $V,$ respectively. Therefore, we compute the columns of $\mathbf u$ as follows:

- First, we compute the vector $\mathbf u_1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 8 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{27}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{9}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the vector $\mathbf u_2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 8 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the matrix $U$ in our singular value decomposition of $A$ is given by

![](images/15/159ace613dacf666b32131543c77b3eb602e16226ba2d37e9e8bea4dcff1cb56.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "04644a93-8cce-5c2e-b575-d7f05b4985df" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6135 :tutorial/title "Calculating the First Matrix - A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "9c32bd79-d939-5ba0-afca-75b88e74b8b9" :step/math-academy-id 37257 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162909}} {:db/id 17592186163155 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163364 :tutorial/content "Let $A = U \Sigma V^T$ be a singular value decomposition of a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ with singular values $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2.$ 

Due to the decomposition, the action of $A$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is the same as the action of the sequence $V^T \to \Sigma \to U.$

As shown below, let's consider both equivalent actions on a unit circle (with the two standard basis vectors). 

![](images/18/18bf28d59138e6c50e950493570a4e9caa8ec2f86eb81d573272cb4677ea1d69.png)

- Since $V^T$ is an orthogonal $2 \times 2$ matrix, it represents a transformation of the plane that preserves distances between vectors. This could be a rotation, a reflection, or a combination of these two, which is sometimes called a **rotoreflection.**

- Since $\Sigma$ is a diagonal matrix, it represents a scaling along the $x$- and $y$-axes by $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2,$ respectively.

- Since $U$ is again an orthogonal $2 \times 2$ matrix, it represents a rotation, a reflection, or a rotoreflection.

To summarize, we have the following theorem:

*Any linear transformation on the plane can be decomposed into an orthogonal transformation (rotation, reflection, or rotoreflection), a scaling, and another orthogonal transformation (rotation, reflection, or rotoreflection).*" :tutorial/id #uuid "4cadc01a-8396-532a-a438-479affeb9a04" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7033 :tutorial/title "Geometric Interpretation of the Singular Value Decomposition"} :step/id #uuid "7cc03796-6cdf-582b-9c6a-edc187a827b2" :step/math-academy-id 42397}] :activity/title "Singular Value Decomposition of 2x2 Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162226} {:db/id 17592186162857 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163232 :tutorial/content "The **singular value decomposition** (or SVD) of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ is a factorization of the form

$$
A=U \Sigma V^T,
$$

where

- $\Sigma$ is an $m \times n$ matrix with the singular values of $A$ (ordered from largest to smallest) on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $m \times m$ matrix, and

- $V$ is an orthogonal $n \times n$ matrix.

The columns of $U$ are called the **left singular vectors** of $A,$ and the columns of $V$ are called the **right singular vectors** of $A.$

For example, the matrix ![](images/46/46b29ceb84e2ed98e48642e67277c9bf63d0552bcd07f813a9ffcaf665ff91b7.svg) has the following singular value decomposition:

![](images/29/298933eb0a789ebe57a296088172f6927d1573770824c0b0cffb393eb9894c70.svg)

The singular value decomposition of a matrix $A$ can be thought of as a type of diagonalization that works for *any* $m\times n$ matrix! Due to the decomposition, the action of $A$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is the same as the action of the sequence $V^T \to \Sigma \to U.$

As shown below, let's consider both equivalent actions on a unit circle (with the two standard basis vectors). 

![](images/18/18bf28d59138e6c50e950493570a4e9caa8ec2f86eb81d573272cb4677ea1d69.png)

- Since $V^T$ is an orthogonal $2 \times 2$ matrix, it represents a transformation of the plane that preserves distances between vectors. This could be a rotation, a reflection, or a combination of these two, which is sometimes called a **rotoreflection.**

- Since $\Sigma$ is a diagonal matrix, it represents a scaling along the $x$- and $y$-axes by $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2,$ respectively.

- Since $U$ is again an orthogonal $2 \times 2$ matrix, it represents a rotation, a reflection, or a rotoreflection.

\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 8 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the matrix $U$ in our singular value decomposition of $A$ is given by

Due to the decomposition, the action of $A$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is the same as the action of the sequence $V^T \to \Sigma \to U.$

As shown below, let's consider both equivalent actions on a unit circle (with the two standard basis vectors). 

![](images/18/18bf28d59138e6c50e950493570a4e9caa8ec2f86eb81d573272cb4677ea1d69.png)

- Since $V^T$ is an orthogonal $2 \times 2$ matrix, it represents a transformation of the plane that preserves distances between vectors. This could be a rotation, a reflection, or a combination of these two, which is sometimes called a **rotoreflection.**

- Since $\Sigma$ is a diagonal matrix, it represents a scaling along the $x$- and $y$-axes by $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2,$ respectively.

- Since $U$ is again an orthogonal $2 \times 2$ matrix, it represents a rotation, a reflection, or a rotoreflection.

To summarize, we have the following theorem:

A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & -6 \\ -6 & 13\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=4$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=16,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-16I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & -6 \\ -6 & 13\end{bmatrix}-16\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-12 & -6 \\ -6 & -3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-16I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & -6 \\ -6 & 13\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -6 \\ -6 & 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{8}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "42130988-8a9c-5c98-b57a-c5c217558433" :step/next {:db/id 17592186428018}} {:db/id 17592186428018 :step/content {:db/id 17592186428015 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "089ec07a-5e86-5e2c-9ee0-7a59f0e9ce6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{\sqrt{10}}" :db/id 17592186428009} {:answer/id #uuid "7011776a-f74f-5038-88b7-bd75d4a9eff4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{\sqrt{10}}" :db/id 17592186428010} {:answer/id #uuid "7450dd95-1930-5564-96d4-6c9e274f1579" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}" :db/id 17592186428011} {:answer/id #uuid "a9766852-3203-5031-bf4e-845ae1f644cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186428012} {:answer/id #uuid "da310c2d-2eb6-5830-855e-93aa19083cd7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{\sqrt{5}}" :db/id 17592186428013}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186428010} :answer-field/id #uuid "01f21526-a5f6-5403-8d94-60d82378f21e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186428014}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "39a1a8bd-f69f-5f36-99bc-5bd95f9b782d" :question/math-academy-id "q-96238" :question/problem "$$

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that the singular values are ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$ So, the first column of $V$ corresponds to the singular value ${\sigma }_{1}=9.$

Hence, we need to find a unit eigenvector of ${A}^{T}\,A$ that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=81.$ Computing ${A}^{T}\,A-81I,$ we get

$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=8.$

$$

$$

$$

$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=8.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-81I & =\begin{bmatrix}65 & 4 \\ 4 & 80\end{bmatrix}-81\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 4 \\ 4 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-81I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=64,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-64I & =\begin{bmatrix}65 & 4 \\ 4 & 80\end{bmatrix}-64\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 4 & 16\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-64I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}.

$$

$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & 4 \\ -4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}65 & 4 \\ 4 & 80\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=8.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=81,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-81I & =\begin{bmatrix}65 & 4 \\ 4 & 80\end{bmatrix}-81\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 4 \\ 4 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-81I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=64,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-64I & =\begin{bmatrix}65 & 4 \\ 4 & 80\end{bmatrix}-64\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 4 & 16\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-64I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{9}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{36}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{32}{\sqrt{17}} \\ -\frac{8}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}

$$

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}.

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}37 & -18 \\ -18 & 52\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}12 & -18 \\ -18 & 27\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}17 & 8 \\ 8 & 17\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=3.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=25,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}17 & 8 \\ 8 & 17\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-8 & 8 \\ 8 & -8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-25I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=9,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-9I & =\begin{bmatrix}17 & 8 \\ 8 & 17\end{bmatrix}-9\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8 & 8 \\ 8 & 8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-9I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the value of $|{v}_{11}|+|{v}_{21}|?$" :question/worked-solution "If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ the columns of $V$ must be the right singular vectors of $A,$ i.e., the unit eigenvectors of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that the singular values are ${\sigma }_{1}=10$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=4.$ So, the first column of $V$ corresponds to the singular value ${\sigma }_{1}=10.$

Hence, we need to find a unit eigenvector of ${A}^{T}\,A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=100.$ 

- Computing ${A}^{T}\,A,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}3 & 7 \\ 7 & 3\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 7 \\ 7 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 7 \\ 7 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 7 \\ 7 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}58 & 42 \\ 42 & 58\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Computing ${A}^{T}\,A-100I,$ we get

$$
{A}^{T}\,A-100I=\begin{bmatrix}58 & 42 \\ 42 & 58\end{bmatrix}-100\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-42 & 42 \\ 42 & -42\end{bmatrix}
$$

- Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-100I)v=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we get 

$$
\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
|{v}_{11}|+|{v}_{21}|=|\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|+|\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|=\sqrt{2}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "eee3bc90-1ac6-5bfc-8f49-7bbeddbe8022" :step/next {:db/id 17592186520583}}] :activity/title "Singular Value Decomposition of 2x2 Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186519991} {:db/id 17592186520525 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162666 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "54deaa5d-b42c-582b-add4-d6575e45a079" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186520120} {:answer/id #uuid "5adca1a5-04fa-5979-ab07-c4374ef39ef9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186520132} {:answer/id #uuid "8584a18f-938b-5b11-9a92-aea06357491c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186520185} {:answer/id #uuid "875c7469-79dd-5306-8869-1ae4d067e4bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186520190} {:answer/id #uuid "e5b0b4f8-5d8c-5df5-bcb5-6a41d1765e47" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186520326}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186520120} :answer-field/id #uuid "50d8446e-fd5b-543b-bc96-f048b71511a7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186161288}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "1290450b-3f65-5ec4-8f81-47e7a7dc9fcf" :question/math-academy-id "q-95734" :question/problem "$$

Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the second column of $U?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ and ${\sigma }_{i}\ne 0,$ then the $i$th column of $U$ can be found as

A=\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}8 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & 1 \\ -4 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}37 & -18 \\ -18 & 52\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=8$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=5.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=64,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-64I & =\begin{bmatrix}37 & -18 \\ -18 & 52\end{bmatrix}-64\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-27 & -18 \\ -18 & -12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-64I)x=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=25,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}37 & -18 \\ -18 & 52\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}12 & -18 \\ -18 & 27\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-25I)x=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{24}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{16}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{10}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{15}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}

So, $\text{Col}({A}^{T}+{B}^{T})$ must be orthogonal to the null space of $A+B,$ which is $\text{Null}(A+B).$

What is the image of $\text{Col}({B}^{T}\,{A}^{T})$ under the action of $AB?$" :question/worked-solution "Pre-multiplying a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ by $AB$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $AB:$

$$
{{\begin{bmatrix}| & | & ⋯ & | \\ (ab)_{1} & (ab)_{2} & ⋯ & (ab)_{n} \\ | & | & ⋯ & |\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{AB}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}={x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}| \\ (ab)_{1} \\ |\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}| \\ (ab)_{2} \\ |\end{bmatrix}+⋯+{x}_{n}\begin{bmatrix}| \\ (ab)_{n} \\ |\end{bmatrix}
$$

Therefore, the image of ${R}^{n}$ under the action of $AB$ must be $\text{Col}(AB),$ the column space of $AB.$

2200} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134834 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135110 :tutorial/content "When considering an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ as a linear transformation

$$
\mathbb{R}^n \xrightarrow{\quad A \quad} \mathbb{R}^m,
$$

there are **four fundamental subspaces** that naturally occur. The first two are as follows:

- The **column space** of $A,$ denoted $\text{Col}(A),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m.$ This is the set of all linear combinations of the columns of $A.$

- The **null space** of $A,$ denoted $\text{Null}(A),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n.$ This is the set of all vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that, when pre-multiplied by $A,$ result in the zero-vector $\mathbf{0}.$

Now, notice that the transpose $A^T$ is an $n \times m$ matrix and can be considered as the transformation 

$$
\mathbb{R}^m \xrightarrow{\quad A^T \quad} \mathbb{R}^n.
$$

So, we have similar subspaces for the transpose $A^T{:}$

- The column space of $A^T,$ denoted $\text{Col}(A^T),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n.$ We call this the **row space** of $A$ since the span of the columns of $A^T$ is equivalent to the span of the rows of $A.$

- The null space of $A^T,$ denoted $\text{Null}(A^T),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m.$ We call this the **left null space** of $A$ since it is equivalent to the set of all vectors $\mathbf y\in\mathbb R^m$ such that $\mathbf y^T A = \mathbf{0}.$

Let's discuss how these spaces relate to each other:

- We have two subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that are orthogonal complements of each other:

$$
\text{Col}(A^T) = \text{Null}(A)^\perp
$$

- We have two subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^m$ that are orthogonal complements of each other:

$$
\text{Col}(A) = \text{Null}(A^T)^\perp
$$

The four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](images/ce/ced4191955b6886491bf612c62344d2faf6e7fe8d49884446de0eb86851d22e8.png)

To see why $\text{Col}(A)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Null}(A^T),$ note the following:

- When calculating the product $A^T \mathbf x,$ we multiply each row of $A^T$ by $\mathbf x.$

- Suppose that $\mathbf x\in \text{Null}(A^T).$ Then, by definition, $A^T \mathbf x = \mathbf 0.$

- Thus, $\mathbf x$ must be orthogonal to each row of $A^T.$ Equivalently, this means that $\mathbf x$ is orthogonal to each *column* of $A.$

- Hence, $\text{Null}(A^T)$ is orthogonal to $\text{Col}(A).$

We can deduce that $\text{Null}(A)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ by similar reasoning." :tutorial/id #uuid "2b6f45b1-7cfa-5c62-9928-caeff36d1cc0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5443 :step/math-academy-id 33937 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134840}} {:db/id 17592186134839 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135111 :tutorial/content "Given an $m \times n$ matrix $A,$ what is the image of $\mathbb{R}^n$ under $A?$

Note that pre-multiplying a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ by $A$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A{:}$
![](images/a3/a3cf2fb6734efe387ad41c59743385154d7a172d2cc10ee0fe69ac6a7f2b342a.svg)

Therefore, by definition, the image of $\mathbb{R}^n$ under the action of $A$ is $\text{Col}(A),$ the column space of $A.$

![](images/db/dbefb436195af5ffa8841f4119054426db50ac2987138a5912991cf42321e0dc.png)

Similarly, pre-multiplying a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^m$ by $A^T$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A^T{:}$
![](images/60/60574ae7f9fc09522e9d725c787dce63228c67e19cbef002b14e29c1f27e4b20.svg)

Therefore, the image of $\mathbb{R}^m$ under the action of $A^T$ must be $\text{Col}(A^T).$ This is also the row space of $A,$ since a linear combination of the columns of $A^T$ is equivalent to a linear combination of the rows of $A.$

![](images/c8/c82ab88289fc2d35ce354933937d908c54a9839bfa0fd126187a9723c58eeb27.png)

We can use similar reasoning to find the image of the four fundamental subspaces under the appropriate matrix." :tutorial/id #uuid "915420e9-f241-5e99-8274-32ffdfb79b9a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5454 :tutorial/title "Images Under the Action of a Matrix and Its Transpose"} :step/id #uuid "e8b74e81-7593-5f0a-9136-22383330a688" :step/math-academy-id 33950 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134838}} {:db/id 17592186134840 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135112 :tutorial/content "Consider an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ with rank $r.$ The dimensions of the four fundamental subspaces of $A$ are as follows:

- $\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A)) = r.$ Since the column space is the span of the columns of $A,$ its dimension is the number of linearly independent columns which, by Gaussian elimination, is $\text{rank}(A)=r.$

- $\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T)) = r.$ It can be shown that the dimension of the row space of $A$ also equals $r.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(A^T)=\text{rank}(A)=r.$

- $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = n-r.$ Since $\text{Null}(A)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ in $\mathbb{R}^n,$ we have that

$$
\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = \underbrace{\text{dim}(\mathbb{R}^n)}_{n} - \underbrace{\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T))}_{r} = n-r.
$$

- $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A^T)) = m-r.$ Since $\text{Null}(A^T)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A)$ in $\mathbb{R}^m,$ we have that

$$
\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A^T)) = \underbrace{\text{dim}(\mathbb{R}^m)}_{m} - \underbrace{\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A))}_{r} = m-r.
$$

Let's add these dimensions to the diagram below.

![](images/1c/1c550b87048bba6a7c362f00f09faca74ca9b056a93698436d0994c120971356.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "40af35b2-abb6-59b8-999a-9976edbb9ce8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5455 :tutorial/title "Dimensions of the Four Fundamental Subspaces"} :step/id #uuid "957cde37-32d4-515e-ad96-75c96f7bfa57" :step/math-academy-id 33951 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134837}} {:db/id 17592186134841 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135113 :tutorial/content "Let's review what we have learned in this lesson.

- $\text{Col}(A^T)$ and $\text{Null}(A)$ are subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with dimensions $r$ and $n-r,$ respectively.

- $\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A)) = r.$ Since the column space is the span of the columns of $A,$ its dimension is the number of linearly independent columns which, by Gaussian elimination, is $\text{rank}(A)=r.$

- $\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T)) = r.$ It can be shown that the dimension of the row space of $A$ also equals $r.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(A^T)=\text{rank}(A)=r.$

- $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = n-r.$ Since $\text{Null}(A)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ in $\mathbb{R}^n,$ we have that

$$
\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = \underbrace{\text{dim}(\mathbb{R}^n)}_{n} - \underbrace{\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T))}_{r} = n-r.
$$

- $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A^T)) = m-r.$ Since $\text{Null}(A^T)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A)$ in $\mathbb{R}^m,$ we have that

$$
\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A^T)) = \underbrace{\text{dim}(\mathbb{R}^m)}_{m} - \underbrace{\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A))}_{r} = m-r.
$$

Let's add these dimensions to the diagram below.

![](images/1c/1c550b87048bba6a7c362f00f09faca74ca9b056a93698436d0994c120971356.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "40af35b2-abb6-59b8-999a-9976edbb9ce8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5455 :tutorial/title "Dimensions of the Four Fundamental Subspaces"} :step/id #uuid "957cde37-32d4-515e-ad96-75c96f7bfa57" :step/math-academy-id 33951 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134837}} {:db/id 17592186135111 :tutorial/content "Given an $m \times n$ matrix $A,$ what is the image of $\mathbb{R}^n$ under $A?$

Note that pre-multiplying a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ by $A$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A{:}$
![](images/a3/a3cf2fb6734efe387ad41c59743385154d7a172d2cc10ee0fe69ac6a7f2b342a.svg)

Therefore, by definition, the image of $\mathbb{R}^n$ under the action of $A$ is $\text{Col}(A),$ the column space of $A.$

![](images/db/dbefb436195af5ffa8841f4119054426db50ac2987138a5912991cf42321e0dc.png)

Similarly, pre-multiplying a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^m$ by $A^T$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A^T{:}$
![](images/60/60574ae7f9fc09522e9d725c787dce63228c67e19cbef002b14e29c1f27e4b20.svg)

Therefore, the image of $\mathbb{R}^m$ under the action of $A^T$ must be $\text{Col}(A^T).$ This is also the row space of $A,$ since a linear combination of the columns of $A^T$ is equivalent to a linear combination of the rows of $A.$

![](images/c8/c82ab88289fc2d35ce354933937d908c54a9839bfa0fd126187a9723c58eeb27.png)

We can use similar reasoning to find the image of the four fundamental subspaces under the appropriate matrix." :tutorial/id #uuid "915420e9-f241-5e99-8274-32ffdfb79b9a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5454 :tutorial/title "Images Under the Action of a Matrix and Its Transpose"} {:db/id 17592186135112 :tutorial/content "Consider an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ with rank $r.$ The dimensions of the four fundamental subspaces of $A$ are as follows:

- $\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T)) = r.$ It can be shown that the dimension of the row space of $A$ also equals $r.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(A^T)=\text{rank}(A)=r.$

- $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = n-r.$ Since $\text{Null}(A)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ in $\mathbb{R}^n,$ we have that

$$
\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = \underbrace{\text{dim}(\mathbb{R}^n)}_{n} - \underbrace{\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T))}_{r} = n-r.
$$

- $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A^T)) = m-r.$ Since $\text{Null}(A^T)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A)$ in $\mathbb{R}^m,$ we have that

$$
\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A^T)) = \underbrace{\text{dim}(\mathbb{R}^m)}_{m} - \underbrace{\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A))}_{r} = m-r.
$$

Let's add these dimensions to the diagram below.

![](images/1c/1c550b87048bba6a7c362f00f09faca74ca9b056a93698436d0994c120971356.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "40af35b2-abb6-59b8-999a-9976edbb9ce8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5455 :tutorial/title "Dimensions of the Four Fundamental Subspaces"} {:db/id 17592186135113 :tutorial/content "Let's review what we have learned in this lesson.

If we consider an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ of rank $r$ as a transformation from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m,$ then there are four fundamental subspaces of $A{:}$

- $\text{Col}(A)$ and $\text{Null}(A^T)$ are subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^m$ with dimensions $r$ and $m-r,$ respectively.

- $\text{Col}(A^T)$ and $\text{Null}(A)$ are subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with dimensions $r$ and $n-r,$ respectively.

Furthermore,

- $\text{Col}(A)$ and $\text{Null}(A^T)$ are orthogonal complements in $\mathbb{R}^m,$ and

- $\text{Null}(A)$ and $\text{Col}(A^T)$ are orthogonal complements in $\mathbb{R}^n.$

Finally, we have that

- the image of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ under the action of $A$ is $\text{Col}(A),$ and

- the image of $\text{Col}(A)$ under the action of $A^T$ is $\text{Col}(A^T).$

These facts about the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

- **II.** $\text{Null}({A}^{T})$
- **III.** $\text{Null}(A)$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{Col}(A)$ consists of all linear combinations of the columns of $A$, that is, the rows of ${A}^{T}.$

If a vector is orthogonal to every linear combination of the rows of ${A}^{T},$ it must be orthogonal to each row of ${A}^{T}.$
But notice that when pre-multiplying a vector by ${A}^{T},$ we actually multiply each row of ${A}^{T}$ by that vector.
So, $\text{Col}(A)$ must be orthogonal to the left null space of $A,$ which is $\text{Null}({A}^{T}).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

I. $\text{Null}(A+B)$

II. $\text{Col}(A+B)$

III. $\text{Null}({A}^{T}+{B}^{T})$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{Col}({A}^{T}+{B}^{T})$ is the row space of $({A}^{T}+{B}^{T})^{T}=A+B.$ This consists of all linear combinations of the rows of $A+B.$

If a vector is orthogonal to every linear combination of the rows of $A+B,$ it must be orthogonal to each row of $A+B.$
But notice that when pre-multiplying a vector by $A+B,$ we actually multiply each row of $A+B$ by that vector.
So, $\text{Col}({A}^{T}+{B}^{T})$ must be orthogonal to the null space of $A+B,$ which is $\text{Null}(A+B).$

But notice that when pre-multiplying a vector by $A+B,$ we actually multiply each row of $A+B$ by that vector.
So, $\text{Col}({A}^{T}+{B}^{T})$ must be orthogonal to the null space of $A+B,$ which is $\text{Null}(A+B).$

continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,g(t)={sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{2}(t)}$ equals $-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$" :question/worked-solution "Since the set ${{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t)}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{1}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(t){f}_{1}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is an odd function, while ${sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is even. Hence, their product $\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{0}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t=0.
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =0-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134562 :question/id #uuid "2b04e926-3f28-54fc-a52b-7c1f046fb290" :question/math-academy-id "q-98689"} {:db/id 17592186240950 :question/id #uuid "e18df242-9d5f-58ab-883f-e2f596589751" :question/math-academy-id "q-104871"} {:db/id 17592186240955 :question/id #uuid "e0a44c8c-788c-548d-8b09-deb0ad2858dc" :question/math-academy-id "q-104894"} {:db/id 17592186240978 :question/id #uuid "2794de9d-8dc5-594e-8a2b-e907f92bf64b" :question/math-academy-id "q-105100"} {:db/id 17592186240983 :question/id #uuid "645a82fe-e42f-5dc9-9e79-d8bd0747a894" :question/math-academy-id "q-105136" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "09b29cd5-55b5-5722-ba90-23f769345723" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1" :db/id 17592186238150} {:answer/id #uuid "5bc19ba5-b098-5af2-b759-18b7d61fa0df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1" :db/id 17592186238854} {:answer/id #uuid "64e8e822-ab38-5fcf-a7cb-162397992404" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186238937} {:answer/id #uuid "9cd846ec-dcb9-5576-8a82-5cbd0e68c90d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186239418} {:answer/id #uuid "a19047b8-6624-5f0c-b217-a2d6a5d4fcd6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1" :db/id 17592186239462}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186238937} :answer-field/id #uuid "f5a8c5d5-fcb2-5bdd-8555-14fa5c61c1d7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186240761}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Let $V=C[-\pi ,\pi ],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,g(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t)\}$ equals $5\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$" :question/worked-solution "Since the set $\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{2}(t)\}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{2}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(t){f}_{2}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =5{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t-4{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is an odd function, while $\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is even. Hence, their product $\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =-4{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) & =\frac{-4{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =\frac{-4{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186240989 :question/id #uuid "266d7e4b-76ad-50a8-9040-cff2b5c11714" :question/math-academy-id "q-105162"} {:db/id 17592186240996 :question/id #uuid "38abb364-8716-52b0-b273-cfd769e1ebaf" :question/math-academy-id "q-105173" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133874 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "39692b40-7d68-5ae5-9fe1-0f8b0b2e0d77" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace Spanned by Orthogonal Vectors"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0344b9d3-e2c9-5e68-8387-9d156ec78af5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4t-1" :db/id 17592186238109} {:answer/id #uuid "38d8be68-9c00-55d7-a56c-7befbf436eeb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "t+4" :db/id 17592186238546} {:answer/id #uuid "987f211a-e0b1-5d31-98ab-50e669f1f18d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-t-4" :db/id 17592186239379} {:answer/id #uuid "c9978a6c-0315-53fc-8721-497fe7cfdd44" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "t-4" :db/id 17592186239825} {:answer/id #uuid "ff73caf6-d30c-588c-ba5d-e9b43a4176d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-4t+1" :db/id 17592186240319}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "987f211a-e0b1-5d31-98ab-50e669f1f18d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-t-4" :db/id 17592186239379} :answer-field/id #uuid "9ab72fad-6b2e-54ff-84a2-97ee3410e0b4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186240600}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Let $V={R}_{1}[t],$ the vector space of real polynomials of degree at most $1,$ and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1).
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=5t,\,{p}_{2}(t)=-2t+2,\,q(t)=-t-4
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)}$ given that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{p}_{1}(t)}$ equals $-5t.$" :question/worked-solution "Since the set ${{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,q(t)={\text{proj}}_{{p}_{1}(t)}\,q(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{2}(t)}\,q(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{p}_{1}(t)}\,q(t)=-5t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{p}_{2}(t)}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{2}(t)}\,q(t)=\frac{⟨q(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{p}_{2}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨q(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & =q(0){p}_{2}(0)+q(1){p}_{2}(1) \\  & =(-t-4){|}_{0}\cdot (-2t+2){|}_{0}+(-t-4){|}_{1}\cdot (-2t+2){|}_{1} \\  & =(-4)\cdot 2+(-5)\cdot 0 \\  & =-8,\end{aligned}
$$

  

and

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={p}_{2}(0){p}_{2}(0)+{p}_{2}(1){p}_{2}(1) \\  & =(-2t+2)^{2}{|}_{0}+(-2t+2)^{2}{|}_{1} \\  & ={2}^{2}+{0}^{2} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{2}(t)}\,q(t) & =\frac{-8}{4}\cdot (-2t+2)=4t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,q(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{p}_{1}(t)}\,q(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{2}(t)}\,q(t) \\  & =-5t+(4t-4) \\  & =-t-4.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186241003 :question/id #uuid "2bf55fb2-ca86-5707-a52a-d891899878f4" :question/math-academy-id "q-105186" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a9db971-884b-5cf9-9a84-c91c9fa4fa01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8+\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186238276} {:answer/id #uuid "39658250-b0fe-59bb-a334-a4e517b0d75e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2-\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186238550} {:answer/id #uuid "880b7d31-ec04-56db-ad2a-f754621f1b8d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186239237} {:answer/id #uuid "b1b15087-e383-5255-8efc-84ad43c168b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186239607} {:answer/id #uuid "cd180c30-2f84-5a24-af62-8965f36db06d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186239851}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186239607} :answer-field/id #uuid "51c982ce-3e72-5b74-bcb0-6eb543685681" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186240480}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Let $V=C[-\pi ,\pi ],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(t){f}_{2}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t+6)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t-2{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t+6{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is an odd function, while $\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is even. Hence, their product $\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have integrals over the interval $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =-2{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) & =\frac{-2{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =\frac{-2{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =6-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

The distance between $f(t)=8t$ and the subspace spanned by $g(t)=4t-2$ with respect to our inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖f(t)-{\text{proj}}_{g(t)}\,f(t)‖ \\  & =‖8t-(8t-4)‖ \\  & =‖4‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨4,4⟩}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨4,4⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4\cdot 4\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}16\,\text{d}t \\  & =16t\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =16-0 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}

2126} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134817 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135105 :tutorial/content "Let $V$ be an inner product space with the inner product $\langle\cdot, \cdot\rangle.$ If 

$$
\big\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \big\}
$$

 is a set of mutually orthogonal vectors in $V,$  then the **orthogonal projection** of a vector $\mathbf{x}\in V$ onto the subspace 

$$
S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}
$$

with respect to the inner product is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+⋯+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{n}}x \\  & =\frac{⟨x,{a}_{1}⟩}{⟨{a}_{1},{a}_{1}⟩}{a}_{1}+\frac{⟨x,{a}_{2}⟩}{⟨{a}_{2},{a}_{2}⟩}{a}_{2}+⋯+\frac{⟨x,{a}_{n}⟩}{⟨{a}_{n},{a}_{n}⟩}{a}_{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $S$ is the sum of the orthogonal projections of $\mathbf{x}$ onto each one-dimensional subspace $\textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{a}_i\}$ for $i=1, 2, \cdots, n.$ 

Note the following:

- This is entirely analogous to the corresponding formula for Euclidean spaces.

- As in Euclidean spaces, the formula works *only* when the set of vectors $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ is orthogonal with respect to the inner product!" :tutorial/id
